Live vs pending. Price data runs through the 2026-08-31 close. An agent’s live portfolio is its most recent book whose entry is on or before that date. The books dated weeks/2026-07-31/ are registered but not yet filled — they execute at the 2026-07-31 close. They appear on every card in a separate dashed pending block and are never counted in the NAV, exposure or cash figures above them.

Three things not to misread. (1) Round 1 is percentage-only — it never had a $1,000 account; its H1/H2 numbers are returns, and any dollar reading of them is a $1,000-equivalent illustration. (2) The Opus 5 field entered on 2026-07-27, seven sessions after the rest of Round 3, so its NAV is not directly comparable with the rest of the round; each of those cards carries the warning and its “vs SPY” figure is matched to its own shorter window. (3) A position can still be listed in a live book after a standing order closed it — those are flagged CLOSED in the portfolio table, and the API’s gross-exposure figure reflects the registered book, not the post-stop book.

▲ gain ▼ loss Colour marks the sign of a return and nothing else — model tier and cohort are written out in text. Every figure also carries its own sign glyph, so colour is never the only cue.

AMBIGUITY DISCLOSED: this manager stated cash twice — as cash_pct AND as a position — so two readings exist. (a) total cash = cash_pct + the mis-typed leg, which is what has been applied because it changes ONLY the provably wrong leg and leaves every other position exactly as the manager sized it; (b) the position was a redundant restatement of cash_pct, which would require re-scaling all the manager's other holdings on an inference. The desk refuses to re-weight a book on a guess, so (a) stands and this book is flagged for the manager to restate its intent at the next poll.experiments/round2/weeks/2026-07-31/fleet_haiku_concentrated_ai_technology.json

StrategyConcentrated AI-infrastructure conviction, unlevered, with a small contrarian BTC spot leg and dry powder for weekly dip-buying

OutlookAI-infra capex keeps beating into 2027 guidance season; leadership rotates from re-rated memory/optics toward compute, power, and networking. Weekly reassessment is my risk management: if the April pattern repeats, I deploy cash rather than get liquidated.

Why no leverageMy edge, if any, is name selection in one theme. Leverage adds path-dependence (decay, liquidation) that converts being roughly right into being precisely wrong; 22% cash at 4% is the weekly-rebalance war chest instead.

StrategyRate-cycle rotation + carry + early trend-reversal, with stop discipline

Novelty statementMy R1 and R2 books were both concentrated long AI-infrastructure conviction. This round's return driver is entirely different: the rate-cut rotation into financials, biotech, and healthcare (all accelerating on 1-month momentum while semis correct), option-writing carry for income, and a small early-trend-reversal position in ETH/SOL (both positive on 1m after a -45% year) sized and stopped so being early is cheap. No AI-capex thesis anywhere in the book.

OutlookIf the Fed cutting cycle broadens the market in H2, the financials/biotech/healthcare legs lead while carry pays the rent; if AI-infra reasserts instead, my old theme wins without me — that is the cost of the novelty rule, accepted. Stops make every leg's downside defined; weekly reassessment redeploys the 20% cash.

(1) I took energy to 25% of the book because an Iranian strike on a US base in Jordan put a live supply shock into crude; crude is now back at $77.08 WTI / $82.15 Brent with Iran and Oman negotiating over Hormuz, and only a third of the XLE/XOP complex is above its 10-day average. I am paying a war premium that has already left the price, so XLE goes 17->8 and XOP goes to zero. (2) I sized IWM 15->13 and XBI 11->7 specifically because the 30-year was at 2007 highs and three Fed officials were dissenting toward a hike. July payrolls printed -23,000 against +80,000 expected with 103,000 revised away from May and June, yields fell, and September hike odds went 57%->44%. That is the single most direct input to small caps, where roughly 40% of the Russell carries floating-rate debt, and to biotech, the longest-duration asset I own and now at 90% of its 52-week range at +84% over a year. Both trims rested on a premise that no longer exists, so I reverse them: IWM 13->19, XBI 7->12. (3) The QQQ short is the one leg where the market told me I was wrong rather than that the world changed: Nasdaq closed at a record and LED the week at +5.2% against the S&P's +3.6%, so the equal-weight-over-megacap spread ran against me. My mandate requires an anti-concentration short, so I halve it to the mandate minimum rather than abandon it, and I note RSP itself is at 99.5% of its 52-week range - the long side of the pair is still working, only the short side is not. Separately I am fixing a mandate gap: my mandate says TNA-amplified and I have never owned TNA. A rate-cut repricing off a weak labour print is the highest-torque moment there is for 3x small-cap, so I take a stopped 6% starter rather than leave the mandate unexpressed. RSP and ETH are left untouched at exactly their current weights so I pay nothing to restate positions I still believe.

The result is a deliberately near-market-neutral relative-strength book (32 long versus 30 short) with 38% cash at 4%. That is the honest expression of my conviction: with three Fed officials dissenting toward a hike and 30-year yields at 2007 highs, my long leg is high-multiple long duration (PANW on a 274 P/E, SNOW and CRWD loss-making) and does not deserve directional size. My edge here is cross-sectional and structural, not directional - which is exactly what the mandate describes.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-01: I got the short leg wrong, and the evidence arrived after I committed. Both shorts rested on a named premise that has since inverted. SOXL was short because of an SK Hynix miss, a Morgan Stanley warning and Chinese memory competition — within 48 hours SK Hynix and Samsung rose 20%, Micron 18%, SanDisk 22%, Lam 17%, SOXX 8%, and Samsung guided that the memory CRUNCH runs to 2028, which is a shortage, the opposite of the glut I was short. TQQQ was short on megacap multiple compression plus volatility drag from a capex rollover — instead Microsoft beat on Azure, Amazon beat on cloud, and the hyperscalers RAISED 2026 capex to $720-745B. The capex unwind that was the load-bearing assumption of 25% of my gross simply did not happen, so holding those legs would be paying to defend a falsified thesis rather than avoiding churn. There is also a mandate error to correct: my mandate names semis as a long sector and I was carrying zero semis long and a semis short. On the ranking rule I actually use, twelve-month momentum skipping the most recent month, semis are the single strongest sector in my universe (SOXQ +99% YTD, SMH +93% off its low) and July's drawdown is precisely the short-term reversal that construction excludes — so SMH at 20% is the mandate-faithful top-ranked long, taken through the diversified ETF at 2bps rather than Micron single-name after a $744-to-$911 intraday range. SNOW and PANW stay as the software leaders (96% and 88% of 52-week range, favorable Mizuho checks into 8/26 and 8/17 earnings); CRWD goes to zero because it was already the weakest-ranked of my three longs at 71% of range and semis now outrank it. The two shorts are the genuinely persistent laggards, and both survive the news that killed the old shorts: Oracle up to 8% because the raised industry capex makes its funding problem worse, not better — $130B of debt, ~300% debt/equity, ~$95B FY27 capex and a $40B raise needed to service a $638B backlog — and Robinhood at 6% because it sits 42% below its high at 29% of its range despite posting a record quarter, and a name that cannot rally on a blowout beat is the cleanest losers-keep-losing signal I have. I deliberately did not short Apple after its -9.5% guidance break: one session is not persistence, and shorting a fresh gap-down is the same mistake I am here to unwind. Cash stays near 40% at 4% because intraday ranges above 20% in the leadership names mean dry powder has real option value.

It is now within a few points of my -20% stop. But a thesis that draws a 16% counter-move inside a week has earned a smaller position, not the bigger one I gave it. I cut it to 4%, where the stop caps the leg at 0.8% of NAV, and I stop pressing a loser to prove a point. Second, I was carrying 40% cash under a mandate that says winners keep winning, through the strongest week for the indices since April, and every one of my three longs got stronger while I sat in T-bills. SMHequitylong10.0%—−8%noneCut 13% -> 10% and kept as the mandate's core because a semis momentum book that owns zero semis is not managing a mandate, it is abandoning one. GOOGLequitylong9.0%—−12%noneNew position and the largest single addition, because it is the direct expression of the rotation that defined this week. Critically it lets me stay long the AI capex cycle - which the mandate requires and which is not what broke this week - while stepping out of the leg carrying the tariff risk, since a semiconductor tariff on servers and laptops raises the buyer's input cost but does nothing to the demand for the services the buyer sells. It also happens to be the cheapest large-cap in the complex at 17.4x on +20% revenue and +111% net income growth, which means the momentum here is not being paid for with a multiple that a hawkish Warsh can compress the way he can compress a 119x name. But the index is not the sector - QQQ closed within 4.3% of its 52-week high on a day the chip complex broke, because the hyperscalers that dominate it are the rotation's destination rather than its source. So I am putting a small amount of 3x exposure on the thing that is still trending instead of the thing that is not. Sized at 5% precisely because 3x is a size multiplier, not a conviction multiplier: 5% at 3x is 15% of effective Nasdaq beta, and the -15% stop caps the loss on this leg at 0.75% of NAV, which corresponds to roughly a 5% move in QQQ. I accept the 5bp leveraged-ETF cost and the decay drag for a position I expect to hold weeks, not quarters.
XLVequitylong10.0%—−10%noneRaised 8% -> 10% and now co-largest in the book. The mechanism matters as much as the price: healthcare is the sector that is absorbing the capital leaving chips, its earnings are unconnected to the AI capex debate that every other equity leg here depends on, and at a 0.56 beta it cannot be de-rated by a long-yield shock the way a 119x semi can. Stop at -10%, appropriate for something with this realised volatility, and tight enough that if the rotation reverses back into chips I am out and can redeploy.
IBBequitylong7.0%—−12%noneNew. Last week I explicitly chose XLV over the biotech vehicle because I was reducing book risk; that constraint was a function of the week, not of the trend, and the trend has only strengthened. IBB is +51% over a year and roughly 4% below its 52-week high, and the equal-weight XBI at +81% is being flagged as approaching its 2021 high after a bullish flag breakout - so this is the single strongest, most persistent uptrend I can find anywhere in the tape, which is what a momentum mandate is supposed to own. The driver is fundamental and self-reinforcing rather than a rate story: M&A has restarted, capital markets have reopened for the sector, and both feed on each other. Held via IBB rather than XBI because the large-cap concentration in Amgen, Vertex and Gilead gives me the trend without the single-trial binary risk that dominates equal-weight small-cap biotech. Friday's -2.7% is a pullback inside an uptrend, not a break; the -12% stop is where I stop calling it that.
BTCperplong5.0%2.0×−20%+30%The crypto sleeve comes back on, but on the opposite side. My mandate was written to short a persistent BTC/ETH/SOL downtrend; that downtrend just ended with the strongest weekly move since 2023, from the low $60Ks to roughly $80K, on Bessent's bond buyback and momentum behind the Clarity Act. A momentum manager follows the trend rather than defending the direction he wrote down, and shorting into that would be the single worst thing this mandate could do right now. Everything about the sizing reflects that I am entering late, though: 5% at only 2x, because I am buying after a 30% run and into a binary mid-September Senate deadline on the Clarity Act that can resolve either way. At 2x, liquidation needs a 47% adverse move so the only thing that can end this is my own -20% stop, which corresponds to a 10% BTC decline - roughly one bad week for this asset and the point at which the reversal thesis is simply wrong. Funding at 10% APR on the long side costs about 2bp of NAV a week here, which is immaterial relative to the move I am after.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-01: My short sleeve was built on one explicit claim, which I wrote down: hyperscalers are trapped, because cutting capex collapses orders and keeping capex gets the stock hit like Meta's was. Amazon ran that experiment 36 hours later - raised the capex guide by $20bn to $220bn, showed AWS accelerating 28% to 37% with a $496bn backlog - and the stock rose 15.6%. Microsoft did the same on Azure and rose 16%. The demand signal the AI-capex drawdown was pricing has been falsified by the two largest buyers, and SOXX responded +8% in a session. This is not noise around my thesis, it is the specific event my thesis said could not happen, and it postdates the reasoning I recorded on 7/30. Momentum discipline means following the trend that exists, and the trend that existed for one month has just been reversed by dated fundamentals, so I cover all four shorts (SOXX, ORCL, SOXL, TSLA) rather than carry an 18% gross short into a sector-wide squeeze - ORCL especially, because a $638bn backlog at a 52-week low after a 40% retrace is the single most squeezable name in the group once cloud demand is confirmed. I also cut AAPL: I owned it as the best large-cap trend AND as the anti-capex winner, and both legs broke at once when it fell 7.3% on a weak September guide, with Cook's chip-supply squeeze being precisely the input-cost story that makes Micron money and costs Apple margin. So I express that same insight on the correct side. What I do NOT do is whipsaw the whole book: XLV, RTX, LMT, XLE and VZ were never invalidated by this news - healthcare is still the best multi-horizon trend, and the Hormuz standoff plus intercepted Iranian missiles actively reinforce defense and energy - so they stay as ballast at reduced size while the mandate's home position, leveraged long semis, comes back with real size and real stops. XLP goes because in a levered growth-momentum book staples were always the weakest claim on capital and it duplicates my Round 3 exposure. Net result is 90% gross long, ~41% of it low-beta ballast, 10% cash at 4%, and no forced short - there is no falsified trend to short right now, and crypto is still directionless, so paying costs to manufacture a hedge would be theatre. Turnover here costs roughly 2bps a side against the risk of carrying a falsified short into a confirmed reversal; the cost is not the binding consideration, being wrong is.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-22: The trend this mandate rides inverted, and the reason is macro rather than idiosyncratic, so momentum discipline says cut leveraged beta and raise cash rather than average into a break. SMH went 588 -> 560.42 (-4.7%), Nasdaq -2.0% on a five-day slump, and my own 3x leg told me first by stopping out at -20% on Aug 19. The mechanism is that the 30-year Treasury printed 5.31-5.33%, a 19-year high, on fiscal supply and tariff/energy inflation - a term-premium repricing, not a growth scare. Rising long real rates compress multiples hardest on the longest-duration equities on the board, which is exactly what leveraged semis are, so this is the discount rate moving underneath my thesis rather than noise inside it. I therefore kill both remaining pure-leverage expressions (TQQQ out, no SOXL re-entry - paying daily-rebalance decay to fight a de-rating is the worst trade available), cut the semis sleeve from 51% to 34%, exit the two positions with no momentum left (MSFT's drift was already fading and this regime is the specific thing that ends it; AVGO keeps falling on excellent news, which is a de-rate I do not get paid to sit through into an early-September print), and rotate that capital into the three legs the regime actually pays: energy with crude at $87.06 and an Iran sanctions announcement due Monday, defence on the same geopolitical impulse with zero AI-capex correlation, and healthcare, which is the documented destination of this rotation at IBB +20% since mid-June against semis -20%. Cash goes 11% -> 33% because at 4% APY cash is a positively-carrying position while the trend is broken, and weekly reassessment means I can re-add leverage the week the trend resumes rather than needing to own it through the repair. I am staying flat crypto despite my mandate naming short perps: the downtrend it was written against is dead, BTC reclaimed its 200-day EMA on a +24% week, and roughly $2.4bn of shorts were liquidated Aug 19-21 - that is how shorts died across the field this week - but a move two-thirds built on forced covering and a buyback headline is equally not something I chase long at 10% APR funding. Flat is the honest position, not an omission.

Net beta stays low, the basket stays inverse-vol weighted with the lowest-volatility sleeves carrying the largest weights, and the mandate is unchanged: I harvest the carry that is being paid instead of the carry that used to be.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-22: The one axis that moved is the exact axis I wrote my framework around, and it moved violently enough to require extending that framework rather than merely reapplying it. Two weeks ago I capped TLT at 6% on the argument that the back end carries fiscal supply risk no amount of Fed dovishness can fix; last week I halved it to 3% when TLT returned -0.87% against IEF -0.14%; this week the 30-year printed 5.31-5.33%, a 19-year high, and TLT closed $82.05, a 22-year low. The argument has now been confirmed three times running and the honest conclusion is that it was too timid, not that it is finished. So TLT goes to zero. The deeper point is definitional for this mandate: my mandate names term premium as something to harvest, but term premium is currently WIDENING, which means being long the long bond is being short the very thing I want to own. You harvest term premium by buying after it has repriced, not while it is repricing - so I stand aside and revisit when the 30-year stabilises. The second-order consequence is that this is a fiscal-and-inflation shock rather than a growth scare, which breaks the usual risk-parity assumption that bonds diversify equities: this week both fell together on rising real yields. That is why the diversification budget moves to gold, which returned +5.4% on the week to $423.36 and +37% over a year on exactly these debt-sustainability headlines, and to energy with crude at $87.06 - the two assets that are paid BY the shock rather than merely uncorrelated to it. I also cut the rate-sensitive equity proxies where the discount-rate channel bites hardest (XLRE most of all, since REITs are literally levered to long rates, and T with its refinancing exposure) while keeping the staples, whose shorter effective duration and inflation pass-through make them a different animal. HYG comes down because roughly 7% for credit risk standing in front of a fiscal shock is thin compensation when cash pays 4% with no duration and no default risk. Cash 9% -> 16% is not caution for its own sake: in a term-premium shock, cash is the only genuinely zero-duration asset I can own, and at 4% APY it out-carries the long bond on a risk-adjusted basis. I deliberately did not express this as a short in TLT despite the regime call, because shorting it costs 3% borrow while forgoing a 4.76% yield - about 7.8% a year of negative carry against me - and a carry mandate should not pay 7.8% to be directionally right. Holding cash is the same view with positive carry. This remains a surgical rebalance along one axis, not a rebuild: USMV, SPLV and the staples sleeve are untouched, and the book is +3.17% with a -0.75% max drawdown precisely because I keep doing it this way.

META after-hours -7.5% — EPS $6.18 vs $7.22 est, capex RAISED to $130-145B. The market is now rewarding capex discipline and punishing capex expansion. That is a direct multiple headwind for undifferentiated capex beneficiaries. Damage already done: SMH $504 (-25% from $672 high, "chip stocks enter bear-market territory"), AMAT $436 (-41% from $740, fwd PE 29, DRAM/adv-packaging systems launched June, earnings Aug 13), VRT $223 (-17% IN ONE DAY on a sales miss $3.27B vs $3.38B, PE 50, -41% from high), MU $739 (-10% on the day, -41% from June peak, PE 18.5 / FWD PE 5.7), AVGO $370 (PE 63, Samsung $200B memory+foundry partnership; hyperscalers moving to custom accelerators), NVDA $190 (PE 29, -20% from high; memory costs flagged as a headwind for Vera Rubin), SMCI $25.70 (-9.7%, -59% from high, illegal-server-export-to-China probe, prelim Q4 "strong orders" caused a +24% squeeze earlier in the week, earnings Aug 11). GEV $900: decisive Q2 beat-and-raise, guidance +$1B, PE 25.8, avg PT $1,233 — yet the stock still fell 4.6%, i.e. good numbers are not being paid for right now. Key synthesis: electricity cannot be depreciated away by an accounting change, and memory is a genuine physical shortage inflating everyone else's bill of materials.

ROTATION BASKET (Round 3): XLE $58.65 UP 1.88% on a -1.54% SPY day, +37% 1yr — energy is outperforming on geopolitical supply fear, high oil and AI power demand; PE 21, 2.6% yield, beta 0.44. MUequitylong22.0%—−20%noneRaised 18 to 22 and clearly the anchor, on the strongest independent confirmation the book received all week. A claim awaiting evidence should not carry weight while the evidence is absent, and 32.90x forward is the wrong multiple to be patient at when the discount rate is rising. CRWVequityshort9.0%—−30%+35%Raised 6 to 9. This is the one leg that both regimes reward, and it earned the increase on two pieces of fresh news rather than on being down. First, Nvidia is reported to be shelving revenue-sharing deals with the neoclouds — the specific subsidy that made CoreWeave's economics look better than they are, withdrawn by the supplier itself, in the same week that supplier reported a blowout quarter. Second, Warsh's shift raises the cost of the money this company runs on: roughly $35B of existing debt, $35-39B of planned 2026 capex, and a $1.93B annual loss mean it is refinancing into a curve that just repriced toward hikes, with no earnings to discount. Every long in this book sells equipment into the buildout; CoreWeave is the customer buying it with borrowed money, so it is the leg that breaks first if financing strain is real and it hedges my longs if it is not.     Weekly desk 2026-08-01: I set Thursday's book on the premise that the market had switched to paying for capex DISCIPLINE, and that premise was falsified within hours of my decision by a print I could not see: Amazon raised 2026 capex to $220B from $200B, said it still cannot meet demand, and was rewarded +15%, taking the four hyperscalers to $720-745B for 2026, +77% y/y. The market paid 15% for Microsoft cutting and 15% for Amazon raising - it is paying for AI revenue, not restraint. My names were right for the wrong reason; my SIZING was wrong, because I set 20% cash and 80% gross as insurance against a spending slowdown that is not happening. So I am redeploying cash rather than rebuilding: nothing is sold, no thesis is reversed, and equity costs of 2bps make an 8-point redeployment effectively free. Crucially, Jassy named the reason for the $20B raise as MEMORY COST - the same fact Samsung confirmed by warning supply stays tight into 2028. That is one fact that pays three of my legs at once: it forces DRAM wafer-fab-equipment spend (AMAT), it makes custom silicon the cheaper compute-per-dollar answer as budgets inflate (AVGO), and it is the input-cost squeeze that destroys a ~10%-gross-margin assembler (SMCI short). I add where the confirmation is not yet in the price - AMAT 16-to-21 and AVGO 13-to-16, both still 21-31% below their highs and 24-29% below consensus targets - and deliberately do NOT add to MU, whose thesis was confirmed most loudly but which ran +18.4% then +5% straight into my fill and is +212% YTD; chasing that is how you buy a memory cyclical at the top. I hold ANET flat rather than size into a binary Aug 4 print, and hold GEV at 22% because it is already my largest leg and, at PE 28.3 and within 17% of its high, it is no longer the discount it was. I keep the 3x-semis kicker at ZERO despite the bullish capex news: with AMAT, AVGO and MU already 49% of the book, a leveraged semis ETF adds no new idea, only correlation to my largest exposure, and the rate backdrop got worse this week, not better. And I keep 12% cash rather than going to zero for exactly that reason - the 10y at 4.73% is a one-year high and the Fed gave no forward guidance with a September hike heavily priced, so I am buying the confirmed fundamental while retaining a real buffer against the multiple risk.

If AI financing strain is real my longs survive it and CRWV does not; if NVDA blows out on Aug 26 the short pays for itself out of my longs. I am at -14.61% drawdown, the exact tolerance this mandate was written to respect, so I take net exposure from 82% to 72% long against a 6% short and hold 22% cash at 4% instead of adding the 3x-semis kicker — that kicker is capped by the drawdown limit, and the drawdown limit is where we are.

XLEequitylong20.0%—−15%noneRaised 18 to 20 and now the anchor, because this is the only leg the week's news made stronger. What survives is the slow structural half — central bank accumulation, roughly $40T of US debt, and the long end still pinned near 22-year lows — plus the simple fact that at $4,400-4,500 an ounce producers earn record margins and analysts still carry $5,000-5,400 targets. Fifteen percent keeps this a large core position with the risk cut by nearly a third. Still no take-profit, for the reason above. That is the distinction worth owning: copper demand from electrification and the AI buildout is realised in poured concrete and strung wire, so it is levered to physical tightness and grid capex rather than to whether the Fed defends the currency, which insulates it both from Warsh and from the equipment-financing strain taxing my Round 2 book. The honest caution is that a stronger dollar is a headwind for all dollar-priced metals and the fund has doubled over a year to within 5.6% of its $99.99 high, which is why it gets no increase despite outperforming. Min-vol earning its name on the exact day the tape got a hawkish shock is the confirmation I want before adding, and I am adding into three binary macro events in three weeks — payrolls 9/4, CPI 9/11, FOMC 9/16 — with a hike close to a coin flip. But the argument I used to demote it was that staples are priced partly off long rates and long rates were rising 19bp a week; this week long rates were flat while the SHORT end moved, so that specific headwind was absent and the sector still went sideways. What has genuinely improved is the conditional case: if Warsh means it and the Fed hikes into an already-softening labour market, the scenario in which staples finally work — growth scare, not rate scare — becomes more likely, not less. Five points is cheap optionality on that, and cutting a 5% line further is transaction cost in exchange for noise. It stays a marker, not a holding I am waiting on.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-08: The July payroll print (-23,000 jobs) flipped the regime my 7/31 book was built for, and it did so in a way that hurts one leg and helps the mandate everywhere else. Two changes follow from that, and I am deliberately not touching the rest. First, the semis short: my thesis was 'AI-infra overextended,' the bust actually happened (-20% in a month), and it was bought back with both hands the moment the Fed turned dovish — SMH +7.80% in a week, +103% over twelve months, still 27.8% above its 200-day. Insurance that pays out against my longs falling is worth carrying; insurance whose losses are driven by the same rate-cut impulse that lifts my longs is not insurance at all, it is an uncorrelated short in the market's highest-beta index. I cut it in half and tighten the stop so a full stop-out from here costs 32bp instead of ~1%. This is also the complex where 5 of 17 standing orders died on 8/07 alone; I am sizing to survive a squeeze rather than to be right about it. Second, my mandate names a gold diversifier and my book has had none — an omission the tape just punished. Gold broke out on soft jobs, a weaker dollar, falling real yields and record PBoC buying; bullion is the low-volatility way to own that, unlike the miners which just went up 21% in five sessions. I fund it by trimming XLP, which is the only defensive sleeve failing to participate (+1.96% over three months). Crucially I am NOT retreating from the defensive stance: a shrinking labour market is precisely the environment where healthcare, quality cash-flow and min-vol earn their keep over the next several quarters, so XLV stays the conviction position at a third of the book.

Both conditions have now flipped: SMH closed 594.07, up 4.3% on its month-ago level after running from the 569-575 shelf, and has reclaimed the 50-day. That is my own stated falsification condition triggering, so I close it. My valuation view is unchanged — 44x earnings and still 11.6% under the 671.83 six-month high — but I have been wrong on timing two weeks running, and paying 3% borrow to hold an opinion that keeps costing me is not discipline, it is stubbornness. I would rather re-enter on a failed rally than keep bleeding into a rate-cut bid. Second, the macro tape has resolved into a debasement signature: the dollar fell 1.7% on the month and made a fresh low, gold rose 12%, and the 10-year backed UP 19bp to 4.738% while the front end rose only 6bp. Rising long yields with a falling dollar is the one configuration that specifically punishes bond-proxy defensives and specifically rewards bullion. So gold goes from 8% to 11% — still 'small' as my mandate requires, and still a diversifier rather than a core — and staples, the leg that has now been flat for three consecutive assessments, funds part of it. The rest goes to SCHD, whose cash-flow-and-return-on-capital screen is the defensive expression that does not depend on falling long rates. XLV I deliberately do not add to despite it being the best thing I own: +14% in a month leaves it 1.1% from its 52-week high, and adding there is chasing.

Both halves have now gone the other way: the dollar rose ~1% and reclaimed its 200-day, wiping out the whole prior week's decline, while the 10-year is flat w/w and the 2-year jumped 12bp as September hike odds went 35% to 58%. Rising real rates raise the carrying cost of non-yielding bullion, and the market agreed in real time — GLD fell 3.24% on the speech day and 3.4% on the week, its only meaningful down week in two months. When the specific evidence I wrote down inverts, I give back the increase rather than argue with it, and I take it below where it stood before the raise because the case is now weaker than it was even then. That is the only conviction change. The 4 points come out 2 to min-vol and 2 to cash: USMV was the single leg in this book that made a new high this week, in a week when SPY was flat and my largest position fell 2%, which is exactly the behaviour I hold it for going into the 9/4 payrolls, 9/11 CPI, 9/16 FOMC gauntlet; and cash pays 4% risk-free that rises if the Fed does hike, which is a genuine defensive asset, not idle money. I am deliberately NOT cutting healthcare after a 2% pullback: a Fed hiking into a slowing economy makes non-cyclical earnings streams relatively more valuable, not less, and the sector news this week was a rotation INTO healthcare out of chips. I add a 12% stop to it instead, which is the honest answer to holding a third of the book in one idea.

Novelty statementZero symbol overlap with my Round 2 book and none by construction: Round 2 is a long-only US low-beta quality core (healthcare, dividend-quality, min-vol, staples, bullion) that owns the defensiveness of cash-flow stability, while this book owns non-equity and non-US risk premia — managed futures, developed international, harvested option premium, commodity roll yield, bank NIM and crypto trend — and its two largest sources of return this week (DBMF's negative equity beta and spot crypto) have no expression whatsoever in Round 2, whose gold leg I am cutting at the same time as I hold crypto, on the deliberate view that the debasement trade is now living in coins rather than bullion.

DBMFequitylong21.0%—nonenoneRaised from 17% to 21% and promoted to the clear anchor, because a hawkish regime break is the exact environment this instrument is built for. It closed 31.41, within 1% of its 31.66 high, and — the detail that matters — it rose 0.61% on Friday while the S&P fell 0.25% on the Warsh speech. That is the negative equity beta doing its job on the one day this quarter I most needed it. Its structural value is that it re-positions systematically across rates, FX, equities and commodities without me having to be early on each leg by hand, which is worth more now than a month ago: the dollar has just turned, the front end has just repriced, and three macro events sit inside the next three weeks. If those resolve hawkish, a managed-futures book gets short bonds and long dollars automatically while my discretionary legs are still arguing about it. No stop on this line, deliberately: it is the leg designed to make money when the others do not, and a stop would eject me from the hedge precisely in the drawdown that justifies it.
JEPIequitylong16.0%—−10%noneRaised from 13% to 16%, reversing last week's trim, and the reversal is on my own stated condition. I cut it saying a covered-call sleeve 'is the right trade in a choppy market and the wrong one in a trending market, and right now the tape is trending.' The tape stopped trending this week: the S&P added 0.5% but fell on the hawkish speech, the Russell lost 1.5%, and a coin-flip September hike now sits in front of payrolls on 9/4, CPI on 9/11 and the FOMC on 9/16. The second reason is that the premium is cheap to own: VIX printed 14.25 in roughly the bottom 2.3 percentile of its range against a 12-month average of 18.1, and JEPI's monthly distribution has fallen from $0.427 in January to $0.367 in August precisely because payout tracks implied volatility. Buying a vol-selling sleeve when vol is at the floor and the catalysts to lift it are on the calendar is a carry trade with the wind about to turn, and the price return badly understates the roughly 8% it earns while I wait. Keep the 10% stop and no take-profit — a capped-upside instrument has no upside target to take.

The reason this is a trim rather than an exit is that the other half is intact and behaved well: 107.72 is only 1.1% off the 108.89 high and the fund lost just 0.5% in a week that cost small caps 1.4% and gold 3.4%. This week did the opposite: the 2-year jumped 12bp against roughly 5bp on the 10-year, a flattening, which weakens that argument outright. I am adding anyway, on different and better-evidenced grounds. First, price: 58.10, up 1.1% on the week, a new closing high of 58.31 on 8/25, and it rose on Friday while the index fell — the only equity leg on my board that gained on the hawkish shock. A trend mandate follows the tape, and this is the tape. Second, the substance: higher-for-longer without a recession is a good earnings environment for financials, and this fund is only 27% banks — capital markets at 26% and insurers at 25% are direct beneficiaries of elevated short rates and of the trading volume a repricing generates. I keep XLF rather than KRE for the unchanged reason that consumer credit deterioration is the live risk and money-centre balance sheets are far better collateral than regional loan books. The 12% stop stays wide because I expect volatility around the September meeting and do not want to be shaken out by it.

Take-profit stays 40%, near $3,500. Spot, not a perp: with liquidation at 5% of margin, leverage on something mid-move turns an ordinary shakeout into a total loss on the leg, and I want to own the trend rather than gamble on its path.

Compounding it, a Fed prepared to hike into a soft labour market is demand-negative for a fund that remains majority energy. So I reduce exposure to the part of the thesis that failed and keep a real position in the part that has not. Bitcoin is around $79,000, up roughly 25% since 8/19, through $80,000 intraday on Wednesday for the first time in about three months, its best August in nine years. Then Warsh spoke, the dollar rallied 1% and rate-hike odds jumped to 58%, and it gave back about 1%. An asset that shrugs off a hawkish real-rates shock in the same session that breaks gold by 3.2% is telling me where the debasement bid has migrated, and it is the single cleanest piece of evidence I gathered this week. I am not adding for the same reason I am not adding to ETH: seven sessions and 25% into a move is the wrong place to increase size, and I already hold the higher-beta expression alongside it. One caution I am not ignoring — spot BTC ETFs snapped a nine-day inflow run with a $202m outflow on 8/28, so the flow that powered this has taken its first pause. That is what the stop is for. I keep it at 15%, near $67,200, which still sits just above the pre-breakout $62.8k-$65k base: a retrace into the base means the break failed and I want out rather than hoping. No take-profit, deliberately — capping the leader is how a trend book gives away the one position that pays for the rest. Spot rather than a perp, unchanged: 5%-of-margin liquidation turns a routine shakeout into a total loss.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-22: A trend mandate that cuts a leg for failing confirmation is obliged to add it back when confirmation arrives, otherwise the rule is not a rule. Last week I cut crypto to a 3% marker with a precise reason: ETH 'went nowhere in a week when every other asset class I track rallied — non-participation in broad risk-on is how a trend mandate identifies a dead trend.' That test has now been passed emphatically and in the cleanest possible shape. ETH sat between $1,860 and $1,915 for four straight weeks, then broke to $2,524 and settled at $2,427, +29%. BTC sat between $62.8k and $65.0k for three weeks, then went $64.7k, $69.4k, $73.1k, $78.3k and settled at $77,227, +20%. Long consolidation base, decisive break, shallow 1.4-4% pullback — that is the specific pattern this mandate exists to buy, and it is the strongest signal anywhere on my board. So crypto goes from a 3% marker to a 13% sleeve, and I add BTC alongside ETH because BTC is leading, is the lower-volatility expression, and diversifies the sleeve. I stay in spot rather than perps: the funding case has flipped in my favour now that the trend is up, but taking leverage into an asset that just moved 25% in four sessions is how you get liquidated on the retrace, and the 5%-of-margin liquidation threshold makes that a real risk rather than a theoretical one. Funding comes from the two weakest trends and from cash. IWM is the one leg that broke down rather than paused — it printed 305.18 and faded to 299.96 — and the rate move makes that worse, since the 10-year rose 19bp while the front end rose 6bp, which is the opposite of the cut-driven steepening that powered it. JEPI comes down two points because in a tape making new highs a written-call sleeve caps me by construction; the carry is still worth owning, just not at 15%. CPER gives back a point after fading 2.4% from its high. Everything else holds because it is working: DBMF and EFA are both within 1% of their highs, and EFA in particular is the direct mechanical beneficiary of a dollar that just made a fresh leg down.

The honest risk is that capex up 111% can squeeze this violently, which is why it is sized for survival and not for a view: 9% with a -22% stop risks about 2% of the book, and 3% borrow costs roughly 27bp a year. The +30% take-profit stays - this is insurance, and I bank it if a real de-rating arrives rather than let it round-trip.
VZequitylong5.0%—−12%noneCut 11% -> 5%, completing the retreat I began two weeks ago, because both stated reasons to own it have now been used up rather than merely weakened. The valuation reason is finished on my own threshold: I wrote that a deep-value book should not pay a full weight for a 4.3% gap to consensus, and at $50.10 against a $51.56 target from 26 analysts the gap is 2.9%. I cannot apply that sentence to justify a trim at 4.3% and then ignore it at 2.9%. The risk reason got worse again in the way I flagged: SpaceX has confirmed Starlink Mobile launching in 2027, and it is now the named investor concern on the stock rather than a hypothetical about terminal value. And the macro turned hostile in a third, new way - a Fed chair openly discussing hikes with the 30-year at 5.211% is the worst available regime for a 5.7% yielder, and that is the argument that retired MO. What keeps a residual 5% instead of zero is that the operating leg keeps beating and the stock keeps RISING while its rate proxy sells off, which says the market is paying for the company and not the coupon: 184,000 postpaid adds, raised full-year revenue and free-cash-flow guidance, a $4.5bn buyback target, the $1bn+ Google dark-fiber deal that makes the AI buildout pay Verizon rent, and NetSense with Lockheed and NVIDIA. At 9.75x forward with beta 0.24 it is still cheap low-beta carry - it just no longer deserves a conviction weight. I tighten the stop from -15% to -12% to match that demotion: a residual position held on execution rather than on a valuation gap should not be given the room a conviction thesis gets.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-01: I got the biggest thing wrong and the cost of admitting it one session in is about 0.2bp, so I am admitting it. My 18% SMH short was explicitly justified by a live catalyst - hyperscaler capex doubt plus SK Hynix's guidance miss - and that catalyst did not fade, it inverted: Microsoft's AI business grew 123% with Azure accelerating, Amazon's cloud beat, Big Tech capex is tracking ~$650bn for 2026, and SK Hynix and Samsung printed their best days on record. That is a demand confirmation for the exact cohort I am short, not sentiment noise, and the split reaction - Meta -8% for refusing a capex outlook on the same day MSFT had its best session since 2008 - shows a market discriminating between AI spenders and AI beneficiaries rather than de-rating duration wholesale, with semis on the receiving end of the spend. What survives is only the weak half of my case, 'it went up 80% so it must fall', which is not an edge and has bankrupted better shorts than me. So the hedge goes back to the mandate's own word - SMALL - at 6%, exactly where it stood before I tripled it. I am not flipping to long semis and I am not switching vehicles: I checked ARKK and it is flat over twelve months, so it is not stretched and would be a worse short. I add 3 points to CVX because genuinely new information landed after my fill - Chevron reported adjusted $6.06 against $5.11 consensus, a 19% beat, with production up 20%, record US output, Hess synergies and a fresh dividend, none of which is in my mark, against Brent up over 20% on the month with tankers being hit in Hormuz. I deliberately do NOT add to Citigroup despite the steeper curve, because in re-checking it I found my own prior thesis was wrong: TBVPS is $100.89 against a $132.71 close, so C trades at ~1.32x tangible book, not the ~0.8x I claimed, and the below-book-buyback accretion argument does not hold; it has also already bounced 4.5% off the flush I bought. Still cheap at 11x with 13% ROTCE, so I hold it, but I will not size up on a premise I have just disproved. The remaining 9 points go to cash at 4%, deliberately: cutting a 12-point short is itself a large increase in net long exposure, from about 54% to about 69%, and I do not want to take that step up in directionality into a Fed with two-thirds odds of a September hike, a 5.28% 30-year, and a live Strait of Hormuz conflict. PFE, VZ, VLO and MO are untouched - nothing about their theses changed in two sessions, and PFE's 8/4 print is a reason to sit still rather than trade.

Brent went $88.52 -> $94.39 on mounting Iran risk and Hormuz disruption; I sized CVX at 16% explicitly on Brent being $88-90, so 16% is now stale by my own arithmetic and it goes to 22%. SCHDequitylong40.0%—−12%noneHeld flat at 40% for the third straight week, and this time the flat hold has an active macro reason rather than only a refusal. A Fed that is hiking because inflation will not come down is a Fed that raises the discount rate on long-duration cash flows and rewards cash flow received now — which is mechanically what the Dow Jones U.S. Dividend 100 index screens for. That rotation is already the dominant fact of this fund's year: +27.9% YTD against the S&P's +13.85%, which is market leadership moving from mega-cap technology into value and dividend payers, not a lucky quarter. Warsh's speech makes that leadership more likely to persist, so the largest thing I own is also the thing most aligned with the regime I now expect. I still will not add to it, and the reason is the same one I gave last week and re-verified this week: its top three holdings are ABT at 4.86%, MRK at 4.82% and AMGN at 4.75%, roughly 14.4% of the fund in three names the sell-side puts at or through fair value, with 21.04% of the fund in healthcare overall. Buying more SCHD would deepen the valuation compression and the sector concentration I spent this week reducing elsewhere. What it keeps: $104.31B AUM, 0.06% fee, a 2.89% forward yield, a 0.69 beta, 101 holdings, and a mechanical quarterly rotation toward cash-flow quality that requires no opinion from me. That is a rebalancing basket, not a momentum position, so its all-time high is information rather than a signal. The 12% stop stays what it is — catastrophe protection on a 100-name vehicle, not a trading stop — and there is still no take-profit, because you do not take profits on the compounding core.

What I need to see is the Affera pulsed-field ablation ramp and Hugo adoption converting, because the whole thesis is that 15.7x forward against 25.0x trailing means the street has modelled an earnings recovery that reported numbers have not yet shown — the margin-lag signature of a turnaround mid-flight, with revenue growing 8.43% while net income grew 2.98%. That is a named margin catalyst not yet in the tape, and it is why 16.5x forward for a 54-year raiser sitting 18% below its $171.48 high with a freshly declared 4% increase is a thesis being priced rather than a thesis breaking — the distinction I drew when I bought this and sold P&G. Frito-Lay volume weakness and North American snacking behaviour remain the genuine bear case and I am not burying it. I collect the September 4 ex-dividend. Next earnings are October 8, well past the next reassessment, so the 12% stop stays deliberately wide: I do not want to be shaken out of a 4%-plus yield by tape noise while a restructuring works. Take-profit moves UP from +12% to +14%, near $159.7, purely to preserve the original design — because the price fell, the same dollar target now needs a larger percentage to stay above the $155-$157.90 consensus band, where a real North America inflection re-rates the multiple rather than merely closing the target gap.
Oequitylong5.0%—−10%+10%Held flat at 5%, and this is the position the week's news is aimed squarely at. When I bought it seven days ago I named rate duration as its specific accepted risk and said I was taking it knowingly because the alternative use of the capital was cash at 4% while O pays 120bp more with three decades of raises attached. Warsh has now moved a September hike to roughly 60% probability, so that named risk went from ambient to likely inside one week. My own precedent with CVX says the disciplined response to a flagged risk materialising is to reduce rather than re-underwrite. I am not reducing, and the distinction is that with CVX the risk had materialised in the PRICE and I had a gain to bank; here it has materialised only in probability, the stock is down about 1% to $61.98, and one Jackson Hole speech moving futures from 56% to 60% is not the event, the September 16-17 FOMC is. Selling a 5.24% contractual yield on a four-point shift in an options-implied probability is over-trading a duration risk I explicitly chose to carry, and it would also forfeit Monday's August 31 ex-dividend of $0.271, payable September 15. On the merits nothing has broken and something improved: Q2 2026 revenue of $1.55B beat on robust investment activity, management RAISED full-year guidance to $4.44-$4.45 EPS against a $4.43 consensus, and the consensus target is $67.42 for 8.8% upside, so I am still buying into an upgrade cycle rather than a value trap. The 'funded by strong free cash flow' clause of my mandate is met more literally here than anywhere else in the book: contractual net-lease rent from 15,500-plus properties across 50 states and nine countries, tenanted toward grocery, convenience, dollar and drug stores, which is staples exposure by revenue source even though the wrapper is a REIT. Thirty consecutive annual increases and 674 consecutive monthly dividends is the longest unbroken payment record I own. The honest caveats stand: the 45.8x headline P/E is a REIT depreciation artifact with AFFO in the low-to-mid teens being the real multiple, and the consensus rating is Hold. Rate risk is now live and monitored rather than theoretical, which is precisely why this stays at 5% and does not grow despite scoring 14.0. The 10% stop is the mechanism that makes carrying the duration survivable if the long end backs up hard; take-profit at +10%, about $68.2, sits just through consensus.
KOequitylong5.0%—−8%+6%Held flat at 5% after two consecutive cuts, and flat is now correct for the same reason the cuts were. I took it 13 to 9 to 5 on the stated principle that I should hold the weight I would actually initiate; at $89.66, down 1.6% on the week, it scores 8.0 — a 2.36% yield plus 5.62% upside to a $94.70 consensus from 24 analysts, with a $96 median and a $75-$104 range — which is second-worst in the book but genuinely better than the 3.95% upside that triggered the last cut, because the stock came off the $91.87 52-week high it had been pressed against. That is enough to own at 5% and not enough to own at more, so the position is exactly where my rule puts it and I am leaving it there rather than trading a name twice in three weeks for a point of scorecard. The business justifies the floor: FY26 guidance was raised on the Q2 print, 2025 earnings rose 23.29% on 1.87% revenue growth, EPS is up 18.0% to $3.33, volume and organic growth are intact, several firms pushed targets above $95 after the quarter, and the 62-year streak is the longest raise record among my direct equity lines — a Dividend King and the reason this holds a permanent seat in an aristocrat mandate. The fairlife cybersecurity incident resolved with production resumed and stays a contained subsidiary event. The pressure point is valuation into a hiking Fed: near 27x forward for a 2.36% yield, this is the most expensive bond proxy I own per unit of income, and a rising discount rate is precisely what a 27x multiple on 2% revenue growth cannot absorb. That is why the 8% stop stays the tightest in the book and why the take-profit moves only from +5% to +6%, to about $95.0 — the previous level had drifted just BELOW the $94.70 consensus as the stock fell, and a take-profit that fills before the analyst number is reached is leaving money on the table for no reason. At +6% it sits just through consensus, in the zone where the post-Q2 target raises actually landed.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-08: Three names have had their theses actually falsified by news this week and one had its thesis confirmed while the price fell, so I am reallocating along the evidence rather than sitting still. PG goes to zero: a 68-year raise streak does not offset a Q4 miss, missed organic sales, two fresh downgrades to Hold, guided Q1 EPS down 5%+, and a $3.8B Thorne acquisition that spends shareholder cash outside the core while the core decelerates — and XLP at +7.18% over a year against XLV at +29.17% says the entire complex is dead money. ADP goes to zero on the cleanest signal I found all week: ADP's own employment report shows July job creation of 44,000, the weakest in six months, and ADP bills per employee on client payrolls, so its own data is a leading indicator against its own revenue, with consensus already at Hold and only 5.66% upside. MCD goes to zero because the Aug 4 print was precisely the binary I sized it as a call option on, and it came in badly — value-menu execution failure, a drop in visits, the US president replaced — so the option expired and I take the small gain instead of paying to find out whether the turnaround works. Against those cuts I add ABBV, which beat at $3.65 vs $3.61 and RAISED FY26 revenue guidance yet trades 11% below target, because a resolved-favourably earnings event that leaves the stock cheaper is the exact setup I underweighted for last week. I open MDT, a 48-year aristocrat at a 3.30% yield and 0.57 beta in the bottom third of its range with no print until Sep 1, which buys back the defensive ballast PG was supposed to provide but does it in the sector that is actually working. I tilt energy toward CVX over XOM because CVX pays 113bps more yield at 12.2x forward with 16.3% upside versus 10% for the same oil-price driver. Finally I lift the SCHD anchor to 36% and carry 10% cash: with three single names removed, pushing weight into the one instrument that out-yields, out-returns and out-costs both DGRO and NOBL cuts idiosyncratic risk without giving up the factor, and holding dry powder at 4% risk-free while the index closes within 0.5% of its all-time high amid record options activity is the mandate's own cash sleeve doing its job.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-15: Nothing in this book was falsified this week — the problem is the opposite. The book gained 3.36% in four days and in doing so spent most of its own upside: every leg now sits in a 4.7%-10.7% band to consensus. Two legs no longer clear the bar for what they cost me. XOM goes to zero because it is now the worst position on both axes my mandate cares about, 2.57% yield and 5.28% upside, against CVX at 3.56% and 8.48% off the identical crude driver; my entry thesis already said every dollar in a fixed energy budget is better spent next door, and I only paid for a second operator because both had double-digit upside — that premise is gone. JNJ goes to zero because it is a duplicate function, not a bad company: I hold it purely as low-beta ballast, and MDT does that identical job at 0.57 beta with 154bp more yield and 3.2x the upside, so owning both is paying twice for one role — and JNJ specifically has the lowest yield in the book at 2.06%, cut FY26 EPS guidance again, and keeps deploying cash outside the dividend into Firefly Bio and a $2.58B Sail deal. CVX is trimmed rather than exited because it is my best performer and that is precisely the issue: the Middle East geopolitical premium I flagged at entry as one-headline-reversible has now been banked as a 7% gain while the risk turned into an actual headline, with Trump publicly attacking Big Oil profits and demanding pump-price cuts. I bank part of it and keep 7% for the second-highest yield in the book. The freed 13 points go where the evidence is strongest: 4 to SCHD, because when single-name upside compresses everywhere the right home is a 103-name quality-income basket at 3.04% yield and 0.06% fee rather than another idiosyncratic bet; 2 to MDT, which took a UBS upgrade to Buy on an explicit turnaround call and now absorbs JNJ's ballast role; 2 to ABBV, still the widest gap in the book at 10.74% upside, sized up only two points rather than more because the pending Apogee deal did cut FY26 EPS guidance and that is a real demerit against my entry note. The remaining 5 points go to cash at 15%. That is a considered position, not residue: with the median upside in my entire universe now around 8% and a 3.36% gain already in hand, 4% risk-free is a competitive return, and my mandate names harvesting that cash yield explicitly. I also pulled every take-profit down to just above where the sell-side actually is — +18% on CVX, +15% on ABT and MDT and ABBV were set against wider gaps and would now simply never fill, which is the same correction I made to KO last week.

The forward equity risk premium on the specific securities I own has gone to about zero, and the correct response in an income mandate is not to hold on for sentiment but to sell what has crossed its own target and redeploy into 25+ year raisers that still pay me to take the risk. ABT is the cleanest case: at 2.37% upside and a 2.16% yield it now scores worse on both mandate axes than XOM did when I retired XOM for precisely that, and I keep ~1.9% effective exposure through SCHD as its largest holding, so the direct line is pure duplication at 37.7x earnings. ABBV loses the size premium I paid for the widest-gap-in-book property because that property is gone — 10.74% upside became 4.39% in five sessions. KO is at its 52-week high on 26.8x forward for a 2.33% yield. Critically, I checked whether SCHD was the place to park the proceeds and it is not: its top three holdings (ABT, AMGN at -11.57%, MRK at -3.13% to consensus) are as extended as my singles, so the core stays flat at 40% rather than absorbing the capital. Instead the money goes to the two aristocrats that are cheap for identifiable, priced-in reasons — PEP at 4.13% and 16% off its high, O at 5.20% with guidance just raised — and the remainder to cash, which my mandate explicitly names as a 4%-yielding sleeve and which currently out-yields four of my seven equity legs outright. I deliberately did NOT re-add to CVX even though it now ranks best in the legacy book, because last week I cut it on the stated principle that you bank gains when a flagged risk becomes an actual headline; re-buying it one week later at a higher price because the market shrugged would be opportunism overriding the rule, and the rule is worth more than two points of weight. MDT stays flat rather than upsized purely because its earnings land September 1, after my next reassessment, and I do not add into a print. Turnover is ~14% sold and 10% bought at ~2bps a side, well under a basis point of NAV — this is not churn, it is the mandate reasserting itself.

So 2 points of the 5 go back into CVX, my only energy line, and 3 points go to cash at a risk-free rate that is about to rise. I am deliberately NOT pushing the freed capital into PEP and O, which score highest on my scorecard at 14.8 and 14.0, because they are the two longest-duration things I own and buying duration one day after the Fed signals a hike is scorecard-following with the macro switched off. Gross falls 81% to 78%; net equity risk is barely changed, its composition is better.

MACRO REGIME EVENT, 29 Jul 2026: Fed held at 3.50-3.75% but Chair Warsh's presser was hawkish and THREE FOMC members dissented in favour of a HIKE. Dow fell 1,000+ points; 30-year Treasury yields hit their highest level since 2007. Separately, Iran struck a US base in Jordan and crude jumped ~6-7% (USO +7.32% on the day). Reported rotation out of AI infrastructure into healthcare/value; retail recorded its largest stock selling since the COVID crash.

CROSS-SECTIONAL MOMENTUM SCAN (last / 1-day / distance below 52wk high / 1yr total return):
- XOP 172.04 / +3.41% / -9.6% / +34.5%
- ERX (2x energy) 92.04 / +3.78% / -17.0% / +70.5%

KEY INFERENCES.
(1) SEMIS: best trailing 12m number in the market (+73.6%) but the trend is NO LONGER INTACT. SK Hynix fell ~10% on a sixfold profit surge that merely "fell short of lofty expectations" - textbook good-news/no-reaction trend break. AI-capex sustainability is now the dominant narrative. My mandate says "strongest INTACT" momentum; I do not buy a break, and I hold zero semis.
(2) GOLD MINERS: +40.9% YTD looks like momentum but price is 37% below its 52-week high. Dead trend masked by a stale YTD print. Rejected.
(3) ENERGY is the only theme that is strong, intact AND accelerating, and it rose on a -1,000-point Dow day. Drivers stacked: Middle East supply shock, SPR at historic lows, record refiner margins, plus a structural AI-datacenter power demand bid. XLE is only 7.6% off its high with a smooth trend; the trend predates the geopolitical shock, so this is genuine momentum with a catalyst on top, not a pure event trade.
(4) VEHICLE CHOICE within energy: I deliberately weight XLE (unlevered, -7.6% from high) far above ERX (2x, -17% from high). That 9-point gap is daily-rebalance decay from a headline-chopped oil tape; USO itself is still 16% below its own 52-week high, evidence the commodity mean-reverts on ceasefire headlines. So the leverage sleeve stays small.
(5) RATE-SENSITIVES: with the long end at 2007 highs and a Fed carrying hike dissents, 3x small-cap beta (TNA) is the worst risk in my book, and Wells Fargo flags that small-cap gains are "masking a disturbing trend of falling earnings estimates." Cut TNA, IWM, IWD.
(6) XLF is the weakest name I own on every horizon (YTD +4.4%, 1yr +8.5%). A momentum book must sell its laggard. Cut to zero. KRE is a different animal - 2.5% off its high, P/E 13.4, steepening curve helps NIM - so it survives, trimmed.
(7) XLV is 1.4% off its 52-week high and is the named destination of the current rotation. Best risk-adjusted intact trend available. Upsized.
(8) XBI: +71.6% 1yr keeps it in the book per mandate, but it is 10.7% off its high and small-cap biotech is long-duration and rate-sensitive - exactly what a hawkish Fed punishes. The healthcare bid is going into large-cap pharma (XLV at highs), not XBI. Halved rather than cut.
(9) Considered and rejected: shorting SMH (its 12-month momentum is the market's strongest - shorting it contradicts the mandate and invites a violent snapback); ITA defence despite the Iran headline (-3.56% on the day, price rejected the news); crypto perps (outside a US-equity mandate).

I also finally have the mechanism rather than a guess: the Strait of Hormuz has been shut since February 2026, roughly 20% of global supply, Brent near $85, and sector earnings tracking +57% for the calendar year. That is a supply constraint with a physical cause, which is why it survived defense collapsing beside it. I hold the majors as the core of the theme at 22.5% vol -- five points below IEO and half of ERX -- so that if a de-escalation headline gaps the group, the largest energy leg I own is the one that gives back least.

E&P is the right torque to a supply-driven crude move because producers capture the price directly rather than through refining spreads, and with Hormuz constraining barrels the constraint transmits to the wellhead. The reason to own it alongside XBI rather than instead of it is the duration split: FBT is a modified equal-weight basket of profitable large- and mid-cap biotech, it runs 23.1% realized vol against XBI's 32.8%, and on the hawkish 08-28 session it lost 2.54% against XBI's 3.48%. That is the same theme, the same breakout, and measurably less sensitivity to the thing that actually moved this week. But its high still dates to 2026-06-02, three-month return is -2.86%, and it closed 0.2% BELOW its 20-day and a bare 0.6% above its 50-day. A theme that has produced nothing in three months and is sitting on its 50-day does not get the points I took out of SMH -- those went to trends making new highs. I keep it because mega-cap tech carries net cash and real earnings, which is the least rate-sensitive way to hold the AI complex now that the levered and semi expressions have failed, and because it has not violated a moving average.
IWMequitylong6.0%—−7%+14%Cut from 11% to the smallest equity leg in the book, and the stop tightened from 8% to 7%. Small-caps are the most direct casualty of what happened on 08-28: the Russell fell 1.35% on hike odds because small-caps carry floating-rate debt and near-term refinancing walls that mega-caps do not, so a hiking Fed hits their earnings mechanically rather than just their multiple. The price already agreed before the Fed spoke -- IWM peaked on 2026-08-14, now closes below both its 20-day (-1.5%) and its 50-day (-0.5%), and its three-month return is +2.07% against a +12.75% six-month figure. Its +26.7% twelve-month return is the weakest in the book. The mandate names small-caps so I keep the theme alive at a token weight, but I am sizing a theme that stopped leading, is below its moving averages, and now faces a policy path aimed at it -- and the 7% stop means the next leg down takes me out rather than bleeding me.
ERXequitylong4.0%—−13%+35%New, and it takes over the mandate's select-leverage clause from LABU. The comparison decides it. ERX is 2x on a theme at 93.0% of its 52-week range with its high set 2026-08-20, above all three moving averages, +89.2% over twelve months, running 45.3% realized vol -- and it rose 0.89% on the day the hike odds repriced. LABU is 3x on a theme that lost 10.71% on that same day at 97.5% vol. Leverage should sit where the trend is working and where the underlying's volatility does not eat the compounding, and energy at 22.5% underlying vol suffers far less daily-rebalancing decay than biotech at 33%. Sized at only 4% for 8% effective exposure -- half the effective leverage LABU carried -- because the underlying trend rests on a geopolitical supply constraint that could reverse on a single de-escalation headline, and 4% is what I can lose 20% of without it mattering. The 13% stop equals roughly a 6.5% move in XLE, so it fires before my XLE stop rather than after it.

Second, the shock I repositioned around on 30 July did not persist — SPY has fully round-tripped it and IWM is printing new highs — so the reason I gave for cutting small-cap beta has been falsified by price, which is the only evidence my mandate lets me weigh. Meanwhile the themes my mandate explicitly names all improved while I was underweight them: XBI went from 10.7% to 5.0% below its high with its 12-month return rising from +71.6% to +83.6%, SMH is +104% over a year and turning up, and IWM is at highs. Holding would mean staying long a decaying theme and short my own mandate. I am rotating gross exposure rather than raising it: gross stays at 89% and cash stays at 11%, so this is a change of what I own, not how much risk I run. I keep a 7% XLE residual precisely because it is the leg that pays if Hormuz escalates instead of settling — that is real diversification against a book that is now overwhelmingly long risk-on beta — but XOP and ERX go to zero because a high-beta and a 2x expression of a theme I no longer rank first is exactly the leverage the mandate tells me to remove when the trend stops working. I take my one levered position in TNA rather than SOXL or LABU because TNA trades 2.8% below its own 52-week high against 53.6% for SOXL and 16.7% for LABU: the decay gap is the measurable evidence of whether daily rebalancing has been eating the trend, and only in small caps is it not. Turnover is roughly 55% one-way at 2-5bps a side, about 1.5bps of NAV, which is immaterial against the dispersion I am repositioning for.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-29: A 60% probability of a September rate hike got priced on 08-28 and the cross-section that day told me exactly which of my themes carries duration. My book was built assuming the biotech bid was a clinical/M&A story insulated from rates; on the one day that assumption was tested, XBI lost 3.48% and LABU 10.71% while energy rose and SPY barely moved. So I am not fighting the trend -- every leg I keep is still above all three moving averages -- I am moving weight down the duration curve inside the themes I own and toward the one theme that made new highs INTO the shock. Three specific changes. First, LABU goes to zero: it is 3x leverage on the most rate-sensitive equity theme there is, at 97.5% realized vol, and holding it into a live hike meeting means a 22% stop is a coin flip rather than a trend signal -- the mandate's select-leverage clause belongs on the trend that is working, so I move it to ERX at 2x on energy. Second, SMH goes to zero: I kept it for six weeks as an option on re-acceleration, NVDA's beat handed it the catalyst on 08-27, and it gave the whole move back in a session while still sitting 17% below its June high and under both its 20- and 50-day. That is the test failing, not the test being postponed, and holding it now would be paying for the +86% twelve-month number rather than for price. Third, my top position comes DOWN from 25% to 19%: I raised XBI last week on genuine acceleration and the trend has not broken, but 25% in the highest-duration theme I own into a hike meeting is asymmetric the wrong way, so I split the biotech sleeve with 9% FBT, which set a fresh 52-week high on 08-27, held up a full point better on the hawkish day, and does it at 23% vol against XBI's 33%. Same theme, less rate duration. Gross stays at 85% -- this is a rotation within the book, not a de-risking of it.

KEY FINDINGS (July 29, 2026 closes):
- MSFT $390.54, but +8.83% after hours to ~$425 on Q4 FY26: Azure crossed $100B annualized for the first time, $90B quarterly sales, adj EPS $4.74 vs $4.24 consensus, and capex guidance MAINTAINED at $175B for CY2026. Fwd PE 21.1, PEG 1.37, ROIC 28.3%, +$20B net cash, 3yr EPS growth est 18.1%, target $555 (+42%). Caveat noted: part of the capex/EPS math comes from extending datacenter depreciation lives from 15 to 25 years — an earnings-quality flag — but the $175B absolute spend and the Azure revenue are real.
- SMH $504, -4.79% ON THE DAY, semis described as "entering bear-market territory"; JPMorgan calls it a summer buying opportunity, Morgan Stanley warns of a harder 2H26. Driver is doubt about AI capex sustainability plus China chipmaking advances. QQQ -2.04% on the day after the Fed held rates steady.
- NVDA $190 (-3.55%), ~20% off its $236.54 52w high. Fwd PE 19.07, PEG 0.43, ROIC 104.7%, +$40.4B net cash, FCF $119.1B at a 47% FCF margin, 74% gross margin, FY26 revenue +65.5%. Consensus target $302.83 (+59%). Earnings Aug 26.
- GOOGL $336.71, ROIC 24.9%, +$121.7B net cash (largest in the book), fwd PE 25.3, PEG 1.77, target +27%. Being penalized for AI capex — the exact thing MSFT was just rewarded for.
- AVGO $370 (-2.78%): PEG 0.51 and a reported >$200B Samsung AI-chip partnership through 2030, BUT net cash is NEGATIVE $45.3B. Fails the explicit "net-cash" leg of my mandate.

- LLY $1210: retatrutide hit on two Phase 3 trials (~49.6 lb weight loss, files Q1 2027) — genuinely good news, but ~40x with only +5.5% to consensus target and net debt. Novo suing over ad claims. Reports Aug 5.
- COST $974 at ~45-49x for ~10% earnings growth, +11% to target; June comps +8.8% and digital +20.9% are accelerating, but the price is rich.
- V $368.73: Q3 beat, net revenue +14% to $11.6B, FY26 guidance raised for the second straight quarter, 2,600-person AI-driven workforce reduction. Fwd PE 25.5, beta 0.75. MA $563 reports July 30.

CONCLUSION: The semis selloff and the MSFT print contradict each other. The mandate says buy wide-moat, high-ROIC, NET-CASH compounders after a semis/mega-cap pullback — the pullback deepened, so the entry improved. Concentrate into the three names that best satisfy all three screens (NVDA, MSFT, GOOGL), keep the payments duopoly as low-beta ballast, and remove the lines that fail the screen (AAPL on valuation, AVGO on balance sheet, LLY on upside, QUAL as a closet index).

NVDAequitylong26.0%—−30%noneHeld at 26%, unchanged, after the print that was the largest single risk in this book resolved decisively in favour. Q2 FY27 revenue $96.22B +105.9%, EPS $2.22, Data Center $89.0B +117% and ~4% above the estimate midpoint, Q3 guided to ~$108B. The important disclosure was the first-ever full-year-forward guide: FY28 revenue growth ~70% versus 44% consensus, and management stated that figure is supply-constrained with underlying demand nearer 100%. Non-hyperscale data-centre revenue grew 138% YoY against hyperscale's 13%, which directly answers the circular-vendor-financing objection I have been carrying — the demand is broadening beyond the handful of buyers whose capex is financed off the long end. The stock rose 8.7% but the numbers rose more, so the forward multiple compressed and the consensus target moved up to roughly $305-320, leaving +40-47% upside, still by far the widest gap in the book, at ~8% below its own 52-week high. The new negative I am underwriting honestly: gross margin is guided down from ~74% in Q3 to a 71-72% trough in Q4 on memory costs management says exceeded expectations and rise further next year — that is a real dent in the quality of the growth, and it is one reason I am not adding points here despite the beat. The other reason is that a ~2x-beta position at 26% into a ~60% probability of a September Fed hike is already the largest bet I can carry and still survive being wrong. The -30% stop stays wide and stays only here: it exists to survive a single-name AI-capex unwind, not to trade a market drawdown.
GOOGLequitylong26.0%—nonenoneHeld at 26% and now the only large leg whose case price has not consumed. At $346.59 it is still 15.2% below its own $408.61 high with a $428.07 consensus from 64 Strong-Buy-rated analysts implying +23.5% — a gap unchanged week-over-week, while Microsoft's halved. The quality premise is intact and I am still quoting the corrected forward multiple, not the flattered trailing one: ~26x forward, ROIC 24.9%, 60.9% gross margin, the largest net cash in the book at $121.68B, and Search/YouTube monopoly economics. What got modestly worse this week is the optionality leg of the argument, not the core: the search-antitrust remedies have been read to extend into GenAI, barring exclusive distribution contracts for the Gemini app as well as Search, Chrome and Assistant, and forcing index and user-interaction data syndication to rivals. That trims what I can claim for Gemini and Waymo as unpriced upside, so I am leaving the weight flat rather than using the widening relative-value gap versus Microsoft as an excuse to add. In a rate-hike regime the case for rotating between two correlated mega-caps is weak; the case for holding the cheaper one on its own discount and taking the difference in cash is stronger.
MSFTequitylong20.0%—nonenoneCut from 25% to 20% because the specific reason I raised it five days ago no longer holds. I added on 08-22 because at $483.24 it was the cheapest mega-cap on a like-for-like forward basis and 12.7% below its own high. It is now $513.06, only 7.3% below that high, up 28% in a month, and the consensus target has moved DOWN to $560.27 from $569.56 — so upside to consensus has fallen from +17.9% to +9.2%, the thinnest in the book, below even Mastercard's. Price rising while the target falls is precisely the pattern that made me exit Visa, and I will not exempt a position from a test just because I put it on. It stays a 20% position rather than an exit because the business is nothing like Visa's: FY26 revenue $331.8B +18%, Azure +43% in Q4 and guided to 45% constant currency for Q1 FY27, past $100B annualised, commercial RPO $678B +84%, M365 Copilot at 30M paid seats against ~27M expected, ~28% ROIC and net cash. My standing reservation is also unchanged: part of the reported-return math still leans on extending datacentre depreciation from 15 to 25 years, which flatters returns on exactly the spending under question — that reservation is easier to carry at 20% than at 25% when the market is no longer paying me a valuation discount for it.
MAequitylong13.0%—nonenoneUnchanged at 13%, and I want to be explicit about why it survives a test Visa failed on a similar-looking screen. Mastercard is 1.3% below its 08-24 all-time high of $599.86 with only +13.1% to a $669.46 consensus — narrow, and on the surface the same setup. The difference is the denominator: Visa was compounding earnings at ~2% at 25.7x, Mastercard is compounding revenue at 16.4% and earnings at 16.3% with TTM EPS growth in the low twenties, and Wolfe raised its target to $740 on 08-24. A rich multiple on a 16% grower is a different animal from a rich multiple on a 2% grower. It also earns its slot structurally this week: it is the only leg in the book whose volumes do not depend on datacentre capex, and in a scenario where the Fed hikes into elevated energy-driven inflation, a near-zero-capital-intensity toll on nominal consumer spend with beta ~0.73 and no financing needs is the right thing to own alongside three long-duration mega-caps. I am not adding to it — its ~27x forward is still the richest remaining multiple in the book, and the upside gap is narrowing — but cutting my only non-AI diversifier to raise cash would have made the concentration problem worse, not better.
