    The book was ten roughly-equal lines, which under the old caps was forced diversification, not conviction. With caps gone I am sizing to the actual quality screen rather than spreading. The screen is my own mandate: wide-moat, high-ROIC, NET-CASH, bought into a semis/mega-cap pullback.

    Why concentrate now: semis are in bear-market territory (SMH -4.79% on July 29) on doubts that AI capex is sustainable — while the largest AI capex spender on earth reported the opposite the same evening. Microsoft put Azure through $100B annualized, beat EPS $4.74 vs $4.24, MAINTAINED $175B of CY26 capex, and traded +8.8% after hours. Those two facts cannot both be right. I am taking the side the evidence supports, which is also the side my mandate was written to take.

    NVDA to 26% (from 8%) is the single best expression of the mandate available anywhere: forward PE 19.1, PEG 0.43, ROIC 105%, +$40B net cash, $119B FCF at a 47% margin, 74% gross margin, 20% off its high, consensus +59%. MSFT to 23% (from 13%): 21x forward with 18% EPS growth, net cash, and the AI-monetization question just answered in its favour; I note the depreciation-life extension from 15 to 25 years as an earnings-quality caveat and it is why MSFT is sized below NVDA despite the cleaner catalyst. GOOGL to 20% (from 12%): the largest net-cash balance sheet in the book at $122B, 25% ROIC, and it is being punished for exactly the capex MSFT was rewarded for.

    What comes out and why. AAPL to zero: PEG 3.22, forward 37x, and the 46-analyst consensus target of $321.66 sits BELOW the $338 price, at a 52-week high, into a binary earnings print tonight — that is the clearest bad-value line I own. AVGO to zero: PEG 0.51 is attractive and the Samsung deal is real, but net cash is MINUS $45B, which fails an explicit leg of my mandate; NVDA gives me the same AI-semis exposure with better growth-adjusted value, four times the ROIC and a genuine net-cash balance sheet, so consolidating rather than splitting is both more disciplined and higher conviction. LLY to zero: fine business, but ~40x with only 5.5% to consensus target and net debt is not a compounder trade, it is dead money with drug-litigation and Aug 5 event risk attached. QUAL to zero: a quality-factor ETF is diversification for its own sake once caps are lifted, and it largely re-owns names I hold directly. COST trimmed 10% to 4%: the June comp acceleration (+8.8%, digital +20.9%) is genuinely good, but ~45x for ~10% earnings growth earns only a token slot.

    V and MA held at 10%/11% deliberately. At 69% in three correlated AI mega-caps I want a real second engine, and the payments duopoly is one: beta 0.75, consumer payment volumes rather than datacenter capex, and Visa just beat and raised FY26 guidance for the second consecutive quarter, which also de-risks MA's July 30 print. 6% cash earns 4% APY and cushions the drawdown I am accepting by concentrating.

    Standing orders: consistent with a hold-to-year-end mandate I am attaching NO take-profits — the whole point is to let compounders compound — and no stops on the ballast, because a stop on a quality book sells precisely at the panic low. The one exception is a deliberately wide 30% stop on NVDA. That level is below the 52-week low, so it cannot whipsaw me on ordinary semis volatility; it only fires if the thesis genuinely breaks (China displacement or an actual AI capex collapse). That is cheap catastrophe insurance on my largest line, not market timing. Turnover is real but this is one rebalance held to year-end, not churn.

DDOGequitylong18.0%—−18%+25%Promoted to largest position because it absorbs the NET exposure at less than half the multiple, and because a fact appeared this week that I did not have before. Palo Alto reportedly held acquisition talks with Datadog before spending $28bn elsewhere; a named strategic acquirer at the table is not a takeout thesis, but it is independent evidence about what an informed buyer thinks the asset is worth, and it puts a soft floor under a stock that is 19% below its $292.72 high. On the numbers it is the best risk/reward in the software half by a distance: $236.98 against 46 analysts at $285.18 for 20.3% headroom, 36% revenue growth, 89.5x forward versus NET's 203x, and genuinely profitable rather than promising to be. Crucially the de-rate already happened here — the 18% post-earnings drop on the OpenAI usage guidance is why the headroom exists, so I am buying after the multiple compression rather than before it, which is precisely the opposite of my position in NET. I take it to 18% and no further because 89.5x is still a rate-sensitive multiple in a hiking regime and the single-largest-customer concentration is an unresolved counterparty exposure that can gap again. Stop moved in from -20% to -18%, around $194: with the position two points larger the same percentage stop is a bigger dollar risk, and -18% still sits below the whole post-earnings gap zone so it protects against a trend break rather than firing on ordinary volatility. HOODequitylong17.0%—−20%+45%Added two points because all three revenue engines improved this week while the stock went down 3.8% from where I bought it, and that gap is the whole argument. Bitcoin ran from roughly $72k to $80,258 on Thursday, the first print above $80k since May, on $1.92bn of spot-ETF inflows in a week — the strongest since October 2025 — which lifts crypto transaction revenue. Prediction markets and the MIAXdx joint venture are pulling a fresh wave of street targets. And interest revenue is already up 278% year on year, so a September hike raises the roughly one-third of revenue that is net interest rather than lowering it. That last point is why this is the leg I add to rather than any of the software: it is the only holding in the book whose earnings power is helped by the exact policy shift that is hurting the other four, which makes it a real internal hedge in a long-only book. I have to be honest that Friday cuts against me — it fell 5.01%, worse than any holding, on the day the hike was priced in, which says the market currently trades it as high beta first and an NII beneficiary second, and bitcoin slipping back below $78k on the same headline is part of that. So I add two points, not five: the fundamental improvement is real and the price has not paid for it yet, but I am not going to insist the tape is wrong about correlation on the same afternoon it told me otherwise. The Clarity Act remains a bill that has been called for and not passed, with only a procedural Senate vote scheduled. Stop stays wide at -20%, near $83, because at beta 2.32 anything tighter is noise; take-profit at +45% lands near $151, just under the $153.86 52-week high.

Two genuinely new facts since last week: a $1.0bn buyback authorisation, which is a first for this company and puts a bid under the stock, and Mexican banking authorisations that turn the second market from a distribution experiment into a licensed bank. The Q2 base is a first-ever billion-dollar net income quarter, $2.47bn revenue up 52%, and 22 analysts sit at $18.78 for 31% upside. The honest risk is that higher US rates pressure emerging-market currencies and flows, and it fell 3.9% on Friday for exactly that reason — but that is a translation and sentiment effect on a business whose earnings are driven by Brazilian and Mexican credit card and deposit penetration, not by the US long end or by AI sentiment, and at beta 0.94 it remains the lowest-beta name I own. I bought it back below its 200-day and I am not going to be whipsawed out of a 15x compounder at a local low on a macro headline. Stop stays wide at -18%, near $11.73, above the 52-week low; take-profit at +30% lands near $18.59, just inside consensus and the $18.98 high.

I sized it as the diversifier that is orthogonal to the AI capex cycle driving CRDO and DDOG, and that remains true — but the shock that actually arrived was a rates shock, and XBI fell 3.48%, the single worst day in my book, because 156 equal-weighted small-cap biotechs are the most duration-sensitive equities in the market. Against a Fed that may hike, this line correlates with the very positions it was bought to offset, so the diversification premium I paid for is not being delivered and the weight comes down to what the standalone case supports. That standalone case is still good and is why I keep 12% rather than exiting: M&A activity and improving regulatory sentiment are genuine drivers, beta is 0.83, and the fund is up 80.7% over twelve months. But it also sits at $162.38 against a $169.89 high, so it is the most extended thing I own going into a hawkish repricing, and buying more of an 80% one-year gain at these levels would convert a hedge into a momentum bet. Stop held at -12%, near $143 — tighter than the book average because biotech gives back fast and this line has the least valuation support of anything I hold, and tightening further would only guarantee a whipsaw in a sector that routinely moves 3% a day.
CRDOequitylong9.0%—−25%+35%Cut from 15% to 9% because this is the reassessment at which I said I would size into the print, and a stated plan I decline to execute is worse than no plan. Fiscal Q1 reports Tuesday 1 September, consensus $470.7m and $1.16 against company guidance of $465-475m. The structural case is unchanged and still the best growth-adjusted value I own: 37.5x forward against FY27 guidance of over 80% revenue growth with optical alone above $600m, revenue that tripled to $1.34bn, net income up 805%, 19 analysts at $283.23 with TD Cowen and Barclays at $300. What has changed is that I can now see the shape of the risk more clearly, and it is worse than I assumed. The FY27 guide is explicitly back-half-loaded — mid-single-digit sequential growth in the first half, then acceleration on optical — which means the number that matters Tuesday is not the beat but whether the second-half ramp is reaffirmed without qualification, and back-loaded guides are punished hardest when they are merely maintained. The positioning has also thinned: the stock closed $282.82 on 17 August after an 8.8% run into the event and is now near $233, an 18% de-rate in nine sessions, with hedge fund holders down from 69 to 59 and their dollar value off 24%. At beta 3.23 into a binary event in a tape that just repriced the Fed, a 15% weight risks roughly 3% of NAV on a single session and a bad reaction could plausibly be worse than 20%. Nine percent still expresses a real bet — I want to own the beat — while cutting the single-session damage to something I can survive and redeploy from. Stop stays at -25%, the widest in the book, and take-profit at +35% near $315, both deliberately unchanged: a tight stop through an earnings gap does not protect me, it just converts the gap into a realised loss at the worst tick.

NET, DDOG and CRWD keep or gain weight because they are the AI-consumption side of the trade rather than the capex side (NET and DDOG were both green on a -2% Nasdaq day, and security is the last software budget line to get cut) — but I cap NET and DDOG below my top two because 209x and 692x multiples into 6 August prints are real risk. XBI stays as the low-beta, M&A-driven diversifier.

    RISK. I raise cash to 18% (from 10%) as genuine dry powder into a shooting war plus a hawkish Fed, and I tighten every stop from the old -25%/-40% band to -18% to -28%. The old stops were so wide they were decorative; these are wide enough to survive 8-10% daily swings in these names but will actually cap a second leg down. Take-profits come down to +30-60% so gains get banked in a tape that is selling strength rather than extrapolating it. Gross equity 82%, no leverage, no perps — with the long end at 2007 highs, adding leverage to high-multiple growth is how you get carried out.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-29: The premise underneath five of my six holdings has changed direction, not degree. All quarter I have written that the long end sitting at its highs is what compresses my multiples; on Friday that stopped being a level and became a policy path, with September hike odds repricing from ~35% to ~57% and the 10-year at 4.73%. The Russell fell 1.4% against the S&P's 0.2% because small caps carry the floating-rate debt. I am not calling a bear market — the S&P was still up 0.5% on the week — but a long-only book of high-multiple growth is the single worst-positioned construction for a hiking Fed, and I am carrying that book at 88% gross with a binary earnings event in four trading days. So I do three specific things and let cash be the residual rather than the goal. First, I exit NET entirely. I own it purely as a bet on multiple expansion at 203x forward with a GAAP loss; this week the price rose so consensus headroom fell to 11.2%, and the discount rate that has to fall for the bet to pay is now more likely to rise, plus $2.175bn of freshly filed converts brings hedging supply. Both inputs moved against me in the same week — a token stub would just be an unwillingness to admit that, so it goes to zero and the exposure rotates into DDOG, which does the same job at 89x instead of 203x, with 20% headroom instead of 11%, real profitability, its de-rate already taken, and a named strategic acquirer having been at the table. Second, I halve CRDO from 15% to 9%. Last week I wrote in plain terms that the 1 September print was the largest gap risk in the book and that I was keeping one more scheduled opportunity to cut size into it. This is that opportunity. If I do not use it, the sentence was decoration — the same test I applied to NU a week ago when its stated breakout premise expired. Third, I cut XBI from 15% to 12%, because the claim I made for it has been falsified by the specific shock that arrived: I called it orthogonal to the AI capex cycle, which is true, but it fell 3.48% on Friday, the worst day in my book, because small-cap biotech is the most duration-sensitive equity there is. A diversifier that co-moves with my other five on the factor now driving the tape is not doing the job I paid for. Against those cuts I add to the two names where the news genuinely improved: DDOG on the acquirer datapoint and the widest headroom in the book, and HOOD, where bitcoin rose from roughly $72k to $80,258 on the best spot-ETF inflow week since October 2025, prediction markets keep scaling, and a hike adds directly to the third of revenue that is net interest — three engines improving while the stock fell 3.8% since I bought it. Gross goes 88% to 71%. Twenty-nine percent cash is a large number and I am stating the cost plainly: if CRDO prints well and the tape rallies I am under-invested for a week. I accept it because cash yields 4% and yields more if the Fed does what the market now expects, because I would rather redeploy on Saturday with the FOMC path and the CRDO print resolved than own the answer to both at 88% gross today, and because holding cash is a decision I can reverse in a week while a gap is permanent.

Research notes — free-internet poll, desk run 2026-07-30

Fed (29 Jul 2026): held 3.50-3.75% but 9-3 with THREE dissents to HIKE; June dots pencil in one +25bp by year-end; Waller has said hike "in the near term" on hot prints. Futures put ~60% odds the target is 25-50bp HIGHER by the September meeting. Inflation has run above target for five years (May CPI 4.2%, June cooled to 3.5%, core 2.6%). 10y Treasury 4.70% and rising (4.55% on 17 Jul, 4.63% on 23 Jul). Risk tape: S&P -1.52% to 7,316 on 29 Jul, Dow -2.19%, Nasdaq 100 into correction, Kospi -6%, VIX 18.2. Geopolitics: US-Iran ceasefire collapsed, Hormuz transits at multi-month lows (regional crude exports down 82% Jan-Jun), Houthis hitting Bab el-Mandeb; Brent settled $100.68, WTI $92.36. DXY ~101.3 and firming.

LEG BY LEG: (1) JAAA - 5.5% distribution, primary AAA CLO liabilities SOFR+115/123bp, effectively zero duration, AAA CLO has never defaulted in 30 years; LSTA trailing loan default rate FELL to 3.5% (from 4.3% Sep-25), JPM index 3.04% (from 4.49% peak). A hike UPGRADES this coupon at zero price cost. (2) CLOZ - same improving collateral, ~9% floating. (3) AMLP - ~$53, 7.8% yield, quarterly distribution stepped to a record $1.03 from $1.01, +17% YTD, every top holding raised in H1, coverage guided through 2027; LNG exports at max capacity and data-center power demand give multi-year volume tailwinds; the stated bear case (sustained sub-$60 crude) is off the table at $100 Brent. (4) NLY - Q2 was GOOD (economic return 5.5%, BV +1.7% to $20.15, EAD $0.79 covering the $0.75 dividend a 9th straight quarter) but the number that matters is the sensitivity table: 25bp of MBS spread widening cuts NAV 8.7%. Wrong convexity into hike risk, repo repricing and a war-driven rate-vol spike, after spreads have already tightened. (5) EMB - ~7yr duration into a rising 4.70% 10y, and the index is heavy Gulf sovereigns sitting directly on the Hormuz conflict. (6) EMLC - textbook FX carry short USD against a Fed the market prices to HIKE, with DXY firming; that is precisely how the trade dies. (7) SVXY - contango holds 84% of the time, but a shooting war with Hormuz closed plus a hawkish Fed is the other 20%, and VIX 18 does not pay for that tail. (8) BTC - $63.7-64.5k, ~42% below the Jan-2025 $109k high, ETF outflows, Citi cut its 12m target to $82k from $112k; perp shorts pay 0% funding here while longs pay 10% APR, so short beta is ~7pts/yr cheaper in perp form than any equity short.

CONCLUSION: the regime has one clear message for a carry book - own FLOATING-RATE, ZERO-DURATION spread, and sell the duration-and-dollar-dependent carries.

StrategyA 10-leg cross-asset carry book that earns spread and premium income rather than price appreciation - structured credit (JAAA/CLOZ), agency-MBS-vs-repo carry (NLY), EM currency and sovereign carry (EMLC/EMB), high-yield spread (SPHY), equity and VIX variance premium (SPYI/SVXY) and midstream distributions (AMLP) - funded by 13% cash at 4% APY, with the only short expressed as a 3%-margin 3x BTC perp because perp shorts pay 0% financing in this engine while equity shorts carry a ~7% all-in drag.

Novelty statementI manage no Round-2 book, so the same-direction overlap constraint does not bind here; the genuinely new expression this week is FLOT, which puts investment-grade corporate floaters alongside my CLO seniority so that the book's largest theme is no longer housed in a single structured-credit wrapper.

JAAAequitylong33.0%—−10%noneRaised from 30 with money taken from the leg one rung below it, because this week handed the position its most direct catalyst yet rather than another argument by analogy. AAA CLO tranches pay SOFR plus roughly 120bp with effectively zero duration; a September hike that the market now prices as a coin flip resets that coupon straight up, while the subordination beneath 600-plus deals is untouched by what is actually deteriorating. And what is deteriorating is specific: single-B and CCC issuers are absorbing all the widening, B3 loans have grown from about $109bn in 2019 to roughly $300bn, and outlooks now name AI disruption in software as a channel into broadly syndicated loans. None of that reaches AAA. This leg is also the only one indifferent to the two things that moved this week — it owns no duration to lose to a 5.18% thirty-year, and no FX to lose to a dollar bouncing off 98.56. I keep the criticism I made of it: the spread over 4% cash is only about a point and a bit, and that is precisely why this is 33 rather than 45, with real cash held behind it instead. Wide -10% stop because the only genuine risk in AAA CLO is a funding-market liquidity gap, and a tight stop would whipsaw me out of the safest income I own at exactly the wrong moment.
AMLPequitylong16.0%—−20%noneHeld flat at 16, and for a better reason than I had last week. I trimmed this on 24 August because Brent had run to $94.46 and AMLP had gone nowhere, which killed the hedge property I claimed for it. This week Brent fell back to roughly $88-89 as Hormuz reframed from supply threat to sanctions confrontation and Gulf exports recovered to 15-16mb/d — and AMLP went up, to about $55.31. So the leg does not capture oil spikes and it does not give back oil declines either. That two-sided insensitivity is exactly what I want from a carry holding and it is a stronger property than the hedge I mistakenly thought I owned. What I am actually paid for is intact and improving: a 7.4% distribution just raised to a record $1.03 per quarter, coverage guided through 2027, LNG exports at capacity and data-centre power demand extending throughput, and contracts that escalate with CPI, which matters more now that a Fed chair has told me inflation is not coming down on trend and my fixed-spread legs get marked down by that. The honest caveat is that it sits at the top of its 52-week range, which is why I am holding rather than adding. Wide -20% stop so it survives an oil round trip rather than being shaken out by one.
FLOTequitylong8.0%—−6%noneNew leg, funded from the EM and mezzanine cuts. The problem it solves is that after this week's move my dominant theme — senior, floating-rate, no duration — was going to sit almost entirely inside one structured-credit wrapper, and JAAA's risk is not really credit risk, it is the risk that CLO tranches gap on a liquidity event as a class. FLOT expresses the same three properties in a completely unrelated collateral pool: investment-grade corporate floating-rate notes, zero to five years, yielding roughly 4.4-4.7% with a 0.15% fee and $10.6bn of assets. If the Fed hikes in September this coupon resets up alongside JAAA's; if the thirty-year keeps sitting at 5.18% it owns essentially no duration to lose; and it has no exposure to the B3 and CCC cohort where every bit of this year's spread widening has actually happened. I am clear-eyed that the pickup over 4% cash is thin, perhaps fifty to seventy basis points, which is why this is 8 and not 15 — it is bought for diversification of a concentrated theme, not for its spread. Tight-ish -6% stop because an investment-grade floater that has fallen 6% is not a valuation event, it is a signal that the funding market has broken and I want out.
EMLCequitylong8.0%—−10%noneCut from 14, and this is me paying for a call rather than defending it. Eleven days ago I restored this above where I started on the explicit argument that a hawkish Warsh was overpriced at 42% hike odds and that I had overpaid to duck the binary. The binary then fired: Warsh said inflation remains too high and the Fed has more work to do, September hike odds went from roughly a third to a coin flip, DXY reversed off its 98.56 low toward a 100 retest and gained nearly 1% on the week, and EMLC slipped to 25.64. When the specific event you sized against happens, the position has to come down whether or not you still like the story. I keep 8 rather than zero because the structural argument that got me here is genuinely unchanged and is dated: from 9 September through 4 November the Treasury buys at least $4bn per operation in the 10-20y and 20-30y sectors, doubling its long-end buybacks in direct response to its own thirty-year at a 19-year high. A government that answers its long-end yields by buying them is a structurally weaker-currency government, and this is the only leg in my book paid by that repression rather than marked down by it, at a 6.0% local yield with several large EM central banks still cutting. The -10% stop stays tight because local-currency drawdowns arrive through the exchange rate and arrive fast, and I have just been shown that the dollar can turn on one speech.
NLYequitylong7.0%—−15%noneHeld flat at 7, because the dated catalyst I bought it for is now eleven days away and nothing has invalidated it. I raised this from 5 on the Treasury's announced buyback expansion, and that is confirmed and calendared: at least $4bn per operation in the long-end sectors from 9 September to 4 November, aimed squarely at the long-end volatility that Annaly's own disclosure names as the source of its spread pain. The long end has stopped making new highs, sitting at 5.18% rather than pressing higher, and the stock is up on the week at $23.29. The fundamentals continue to deliver — dividend raised to $0.75 on $0.79 of earnings available for distribution, $20.15 book value, 5.5% economic return in Q2 and 6.9% for the half, net interest spread up 8bp to 1.50%. I am not adding despite that, because a September hike with a stable thirty-year is a bear flattener, which is the curve shape that most directly compresses the spread on a 5.6x-levered agency book by raising repo cost against static asset yields, and because agency MBS still trades at historically wide spreads with the Fed running off passively and banks inactive. Holding is the honest answer when the catalyst is intact but the rate path has turned less friendly. -15% stop.
CLOZequitylong5.0%—−15%noneHalved from 10, one rung below JAAA and for the mirror image of JAAA's reason. BBB and BB CLO mezzanine at roughly 7.2% is a levered claim on the single-B and CCC loan cohort, and this week gave me two independent reasons to want less of it. First, a September hike now priced as a coin flip raises the debt service of floating-rate leveraged borrowers, which is a direct solvency pressure on exactly this collateral rather than a mark-to-market one. Second, the distribution keeps getting uglier in ways that are now documented rather than inferred: the HY index OAS of 275-281bp sits in the richest decile of its own history against a long-run median near 450bp, B3 loans have grown from about $109bn at end-2019 to roughly $300bn, and 2026 outlooks now explicitly route AI disruption in software into broadly syndicated loans and private credit marks. The fund's own numbers already show me paying for this — a 5.05% total return against a 7.22% distribution means principal is funding the coupon. I hold 5 rather than zero because top-of-collateral performance is genuinely fine, payment defaults remain below long-run averages, and floating-rate coupons are still the right place to sit while the long end is the volatile part of the curve. What I will no longer do is take that subordination in size for three and a half points over cash. -15% stop respects how mezzanine gaps.
SPYIequitylong4.0%—−15%noneHeld flat at 4 for the second week, and once again I decline to add — this time with the cleanest version of the argument I have had. My standing objection is that writing index calls deserves size when volatility is expensive and not when it is cheap. VIX closed at 14.35 on Friday, touched 14.1 after the Warsh speech, and that is the lowest print of the entire year; the market absorbed a Fed chair signalling hikes by selling volatility. Selling premium into the cheapest insurance price of 2026 is the definition of getting paid badly for a real risk, so this stays a token sleeve that satisfies the mandate's equity-premium requirement and clears monthly cash, nothing more. The two caveats I have stated before still hold and still cap the size: the 11.85% distribution carries a 331% payout ratio, so much of what I collect is return of capital rather than harvested premium, and the fund is roughly 8% NVIDIA, 7% Apple and 6% Microsoft, which is concentrated single-name beta wearing an income label. For identical reasons I again decline to open SVXY — with VIX at the year's low, short variance is the single worst-compensated carry available to me. -15% stop.

  1. 2026-07-27OPENEDOpening book registered · experiments/round3/allocations/opus5_carry.json

    Outlook at registrationI expect a slow, low-variance grind of roughly 0.5-0.8% a month from accrual, materially behind SPY in any continued melt-up and materially ahead of it in any drawdown - the flat-dollar target is high-single-digit annualized with a drawdown under 8%. Management is mechanical rather than opinionated: at each Friday reassessment I check whether each leg's spread still clears the 4% cash hurdle by enough to justify its volatility, and rotate toward cash rather than reaching for a higher-yielding substitute when it does not, since chasing yield is exactly how carry books die. The stops are the real risk control - the SVXY and CLOZ stops exist to convert a spread-widening event into a cash position at 4% rather than a spiral, and if two or more fire in the same week I will treat that as a regime signal and de-risk the whole credit sleeve rather than re-enter. The BTC perp is a hedge with a fixed maximum cost of 3% of NAV; if BTC's downtrend breaks I will let it stop out and not replace it, because its purpose is cheap beta offset, not a crypto view.

    Run through tracker/round2.py --backtest on the exact file registered here; numbers are verbatim. The book trailed SPY in all three windows but took roughly 40% of SPY's drawdown (-3.65 vs -8.88 in 2026H1, -1.50 vs -5.07 in 2025H2), which is the expected shape of carry. Honest attribution: the largest single contributor in both mandated windows was the BTC perp short (+2.62% of NAV in 2026H1, +2.29% in 2025H2), and that is directional luck, not carry - BTC fell 29% and 26% in those windows, and the engine pays a short perp nothing for holding it. In 2025H1, when BTC rose, the same leg cost -0.70%. Strip the perp and the book returns roughly 4.3% and 7.0% in the two mandated windows. The genuine carry engine was NLY (+2.12% of NAV in 2025H2), SVXY (+1.62% in 2025H2, but stopped out for -1.6% in 2025H1), AMLP (+1.85% in 2026H1) and the steady 2.4-3.1%-per-half grind from JAAA and CLOZ. Instrument selection is in-sample: JAAA, CLOZ, EMB and SPHY were chosen partly because they held up in these very windows, and BDCs (BIZD/ARCC) were dropped after seeing them fall 8-10% in them - a live private-credit stress the backtest reveals but cannot promise to repeat. Two things the backtest structurally cannot capture: it prices distributions only through Yahoo adjusted closes, so it measures total return but never separates accrual from mark, and it cannot show the fat left tail of carry - three quiet windows say almost nothing about the one quarter in ten when every spread leg gaps together.

  2. 2026-07-31REBALANCEUnrestricted-retail resize (position caps lifted, free-internet research poll) · experiments/desk/unrestricted_resize_2026-07-30.json
    Stated reason (desk log)

    The Fed's hawkish 29-July hold (three dissents to HIKE, ~60% odds of a higher target by September) splits my ten carry legs cleanly in two, and the freedom to size means I should stop pretending they are equally good. Floating-rate CLO carry gets a coupon UPGRADE from a hike at zero duration cost; three of my legs get hit twice by that same event. So I concentrate hard into the winners and cut the losers to zero rather than trimming everything by a token amount. RAISED: JAAA 16 -> 40, the single best risk-adjusted carry available - SOFR+~120bp floating, 5.5% distribution, effectively zero duration, AAA CLO has never defaulted in thirty years, and the underlying loan default rate is FALLING (4.3% -> 3.5%). It reprices upward if the Fed hikes and loses nothing if it doesn't. Under the old caps I could not express that; I can now, so it becomes the anchor with a deliberately wide -10% stop that only fires in a 2020-style liquidity gap. AMLP 9 -> 16, the highest-conviction risk-carry and the one leg the oil shock pays rather than punishes: 7.8% yield, record $1.03 distribution just raised, +17% YTD, LNG and data-center volume tailwinds, and $100 Brent removes its only stated downside. CLOZ 13 -> 15 and SPHY 6 -> 8, second and third helpings of the same improving-collateral floating credit. BTC perp short 3 -> 5 (15% notional at 3x), the cheapest beta hedge in the engine at 0% funding, against an asset 42% off its high with ETF outflows and a hawkish Fed. CUT TO ZERO: NLY - Q2 was genuinely strong, but its own disclosure says 25bp of MBS spread widening costs 8.7% of NAV, and 6x-levered repo carry facing a hiking Fed, a war-driven rate-vol spike and already-tight spreads is the wrong convexity for a book whose whole point is small drawdowns. EMB - roughly seven years of duration into a 10y at 4.70% and rising, with heavy Gulf sovereign weight sitting on top of the Hormuz conflict. EMLC - shorting the dollar for a rate differential against a Fed the market prices to hike, with DXY firming. SVXY - VIX at 18 is not enough premium for short vol into a US-Iran shooting war. TRIMMED: SPYI 10 -> 6; still a real variance premium and richer at VIX 18, but it is long index beta with capped upside into a correcting tape and AMLP already supplies my equity beta. Cash 13 -> 10 because JAAA earns 5.5% for barely more risk than the 4% cash rate. Result: six legs, 90% gross, with 55% of NAV in floating-rate spread that gets BETTER if the Fed does what the market now expects.     Unrestricted-retail resize (2026-07-30, free internet + no sizing caps): The Fed's hawkish 29-July hold (three dissents to HIKE, ~60% odds of a higher target by September) splits my ten carry legs cleanly in two, and the freedom to size means I should stop pretending they are equally good. Floating-rate CLO carry gets a coupon UPGRADE from a hike at zero duration cost; three of my legs get hit twice by that same event. So I concentrate hard into the winners and cut the losers to zero rather than trimming everything by a token amount. RAISED: JAAA 16 -> 40, the single best risk-adjusted carry available - SOFR+~120bp floating, 5.5% distribution, effectively zero duration, AAA CLO has never defaulted in thirty years, and the underlying loan default rate is FALLING (4.3% -> 3.5%). It reprices upward if the Fed hikes and loses nothing if it doesn't. Under the old caps I could not express that; I can now, so it becomes the anchor with a deliberately wide -10% stop that only fires in a 2020-style liquidity gap. AMLP 9 -> 16, the highest-conviction risk-carry and the one leg the oil shock pays rather than punishes: 7.8% yield, record $1.03 distribution just raised, +17% YTD, LNG and data-center volume tailwinds, and $100 Brent removes its only stated downside. CLOZ 13 -> 15 and SPHY 6 -> 8, second and third helpings of the same improving-collateral floating credit. BTC perp short 3 -> 5 (15% notional at 3x), the cheapest beta hedge in the engine at 0% funding, against an asset 42% off its high with ETF outflows and a hawkish Fed. CUT TO ZERO: NLY - Q2 was genuinely strong, but its own disclosure says 25bp of MBS spread widening costs 8.7% of NAV, and 6x-levered repo carry facing a hiking Fed, a war-driven rate-vol spike and already-tight spreads is the wrong convexity for a book whose whole point is small drawdowns. EMB - roughly seven years of duration into a 10y at 4.70% and rising, with heavy Gulf sovereign weight sitting on top of the Hormuz conflict. EMLC - shorting the dollar for a rate differential against a Fed the market prices to hike, with DXY firming. SVXY - VIX at 18 is not enough premium for short vol into a US-Iran shooting war.     Weekly desk 2026-08-08: I sized this book on a specific, stated macro call — that a September hike at ~60% odds made floating-rate CLO carry uniquely privileged — and Friday's payroll print (-23,000 vs +80,000 expected, earnings growth down to 3.2%) took that hike off the table. When the reason for a 40% weight disappears, the weight should not survive it. Two things follow mechanically. First, JAAA's coupon-upgrade optionality is gone, leaving a 4.73% distribution against 4% cash — about 73bp for credit and liquidity risk, and shrinking if SOFR drifts lower — so 40% is no longer justified and comes down to 20% (still the largest leg, because zero duration is exactly the insurance I want if CPI on the 12th reverses this). Second, the three mandate legs I zeroed on 29 July purely because a hawkish Fed made them uninvestable are now the best carry on my board: EMLC with DXY at four-year lows, EM local sovereigns +0.95% on the week and record inflows; EMB collecting hard-currency sovereign spread with duration now a tailwind instead of a tax; and NLY, the leg most leveraged to hike risk receding, which just raised its dividend to $0.75 on 105% EAD coverage with book value up 1.7% and spread widening 8bp. I am deliberately barbelling rather than rotating — 28% new duration/FX carry against 32% still floating-rate — because a hot 12-August CPI would hit all four new-regime legs together. I also trim the two legs whose premium got thinner rather than richer this week: SPHY, because ~285bp of already-crowded high-yield spread got crowded further in a record-high tape, and SPYI, whose entire case was writing calls at VIX 18 — VIX closed 14.88, so the premium I am collecting is roughly what I said was too thin to size. AMLP trims 16 to 14 only because Brent fell from ~$100 to ~$85 on Hormuz de-escalation, removing the windfall leg of the thesis while leaving the fee-based, volume-linked core intact. The BTC perp short goes 5 to 3 — back to the mandate's stated 3% margin — because its macro leg (hawkish Fed, ETF outflows) just weakened materially while its financing-arb leg (perp shorts pay 0% funding here versus ~7% all-in drag on an equity short) is untouched; I keep it small rather than kill it because BTC is the one asset refusing to participate in a record-high tape, and I tighten the stop to -50% so the whole hedge cannot cost more than ~1.5% of NAV. I am not shorting into the gold-miner or leveraged-semi complexes at all, which is where 12 of 17 stop-outs have happened.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-15: I built this book five days ago on three stated premises and all three have been contradicted by data since, in the same direction. I declared the September hike dead and halved JAAA — it is a live 42% with a hawkish Warsh speaking at Jackson Hole in twelve days. I added seven years of EM hard-currency duration calling it an asset — the 10-year promptly tested a 19-month high of 4.75% on term premium while 1-year inflation expectations rose to 4.3%. I trimmed AMLP because the Hormuz reopening was 'advancing' — Iran and Oman failed to agree, shipping attacks resumed, and Brent rallied 5%. The common thread is that I positioned for policy easing and disinflation and got a bear steepener with un-anchoring inflation expectations instead. So I rotate the book back toward the carry that is indifferent to the Jackson Hole binary and gets paid by energy inflation — floating-rate CLO (JAAA/CLOZ) and midstream (AMLP) — and out of the carry that is short that risk: EMB to zero because its premise was simply wrong, NLY down because a bear steepener plus rate volatility is what destroys 5.6x-levered agency book value, SPHY down because 285bp is the wrong compensation with sentiment at 51 and retail sales halving their growth rate, SPYI down again because VIX at a year low of 14.25 is the cheapest possible price to sell insurance. Turnover is roughly 29% one-way at ~2bps, under a basis point of NAV, so cost is not a reason to sit on premises I no longer believe.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-22: Two facts changed enough to move real weight, and one of my hedges is gone. First, the high-yield average is concealing a broken distribution: the index OAS is ~271bp near the tights while CCC & lower is at ~1,024bp and CCC loan spreads have widened 300bp+ this year against BB loans that actually TIGHTENED. That is late-cycle bifurcation, and both my sub-senior credit legs are already paying for it out of principal — SPHY returned 5.65% over a year on a 7.20% coupon, CLOZ 5.05% on a 7.22% coupon. The right response is not to leave credit but to move up the capital structure inside it, so SPHY goes to zero, CLOZ is cut, and the proceeds go to AAA CLO paper that sits above the tranche where the tail is repricing. Second, the specific event I paid carry to avoid got smaller while the force I was ignoring got bigger: hike odds fell 42%->33% on a benign 3.4%/2.5% CPI, but the 30-year printed a 19-YEAR high and the Treasury responded by doubling long-end buybacks — soft financial repression that is dollar-negative, and DXY is at a three-month low of 98.80. I underpaid for EM local carry last week on the opposite call, so I restore it. Third, I am not replacing the BTC short. It cost me ~2.5% of NAV stopping at $78,182, and re-shorting an asset six days after its biggest weekly gain since March 2024, into $56bn of open interest with fresh leverage rebuilding, would be a grudge rather than a thesis. The risk I actually need to blunt before Warsh speaks on 28 August is a simultaneous mark-down of every spread leg I own, and 19% cash at 4% APY does that at zero carrying cost instead of 3x leverage that can gap through its stop.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-29: A binary I explicitly sized around resolved against me, and it resolved in a direction that reprices the whole book's internal ranking rather than just one leg. Last week I raised EMLC from 10 to 14 on the argument that a hawkish Jackson Hole was overpriced at 42% hike odds and that I had overpaid to duck it. Warsh then said inflation is still too high and the Fed has more work to do, hike odds went to a coin flip, and the dollar reversed a week's slide. I was wrong, so I cut the position rather than the story. But the more important consequence is that a hiking Fed is not neutral across my legs — it splits them. Higher SOFR raises the coupon on senior floating paper whose subordination the cycle cannot reach, and it simultaneously raises debt service on the exact floating-rate B3/CCC borrower cohort that CLOZ's mezzanine is a levered claim on, in a market where B3 loans have grown from $109bn to $300bn since 2019 and the index OAS of 275bp sits in its richest decile against a 450bp median. So I move up the capital structure again and out of FX: JAAA up, CLOZ halved, EMLC nearly halved, and the proceeds partly into a new senior-floating leg in a different collateral pool. Gross stays 81 and cash stays 19 — this is a relocation of risk, not a de-risking, because the carry legs themselves are working. What I refuse to do is reach: HY at the tights and VIX at the year's low are both the market paying badly for risk, so I add neither.

Philadelphia Semiconductor Index is -19% month-to-date, its worst month since 2008, with every member below its 50-day MA; chip stocks have shed more than $1trn. Triggers: China's CXMT completed its IPO and rose 466% day one (structural memory-supply threat), SK Hynix posted record revenue but missed consensus, and flagship datacentre GPU rental prices fell ~31% in three weeks. Alphabet reported its first negative FCF quarter; Meta reported 29 Jul, missed EPS, raised FY26 opex to $165-169bn and capex to $130-145bn, and fell ~10% after hours; Microsoft reported the same night into the same scepticism. FOMC is this week.

The mirror image is broad: healthcare and financials hit fresh intraday all-time highs, small caps are leading, and RSP (equal-weight S&P) is +3.54% over the past month versus VOO -0.2%, and now ahead YTD (10.5% vs 9.0%). That is a 3.7pp equal-weight-over-cap-weight spread in one month — literally my mandate's trade.

Name-level work on my own book:

- PLTR: -7% on 27 Jul, fourth straight down day, still ~41-42x sales, -26% YTD. CRM: closed red for a record 14th consecutive session on the "general-purpose AI erodes specialist software" thesis. Both are trending, not scattering.
- HUM: Q2 adj EPS $7.61 vs $7.22 est, revenue $40.87bn (+26%); fell 6.7% to $362.51 on unchanged guidance and a 2027 exit from MA plans covering ~600k members (margin-accretive, path to 3% pretax by 2028). A cheaper entry into the leading rotation sector.

- COF (new): Q2 net income $3.0bn, adj EPS $5.81, revenue $15.85bn vs $15.7bn est, credit losses falling, Discover integration 14 months in and on track for $2.5bn synergies by 2027, domestic card volume +26% y/y.

StrategyEqual-weight 51% long basket of twelve large caps screened for the highest idiosyncratic (residual-to-SPY) volatility and the lowest mutual correlation across eight sectors, hedged with a 47% short of the cap-weighted indices they sit in (28% SPY + 19% QQQ, the split that minimised residual volatility across five half-year windows), leaving 2% cash and roughly zero net index beta.

Novelty statementI manage no Round-2 book, so there is no same-direction overlap to constrain; this Round-3 book remains its own construction — twelve high-residual-volatility large caps across eight sectors held equal-weight against a residual-vol-minimising 28% SPY / 19% QQQ index short, with no crypto, no leverage and no directional index view anywhere in it.

    Outlook at registrationI expect a low-volatility, low-beta equity curve - roughly 7-9% annualised book volatility, drawdowns in the 4-6% range, and returns that will look dull against SPY in any strong beta rally and good against SPY in a flat or falling tape. The realistic base case is mid-single-digit annualised excess over cash if the current 1st-percentile correlation regime persists, and roughly flat if it does not. Management: re-run the idiosyncratic-volatility and pairwise-correlation screen every Friday and replace the bottom two or three names rather than holding a stale basket, since the out-of-sample evidence says the refreshed procedure works better than the fixed list; re-estimate the basket's beta weekly and resize the SPY/QQQ short to keep net beta inside +/-0.15, tolerating a small net short rather than a net long given that correlation is far more likely to rise than fall from 0.08. The trade I am watching for is a correlation spike: if the rolling 63-day average pairwise correlation moves back above 0.20, the dispersion premise is gone, the basket and the shorts converge, and I would cut gross exposure toward cash rather than try to ride it out. The dominant risk is a correlated selloff, in which every long falls together, the hedge only offsets its beta share, and the residual +0.10 net long plus the basket's higher-than-index volatility both work against me at once.

    Pre-registration backtest
    windows tested2026-01-02 to 2026-07-24; 2025-07-16 to 2025-12-31
    strategy return pct2026H1 +19.48%; 2025H2 +0.87%
    benchmark return pct2026H1_SPY +8.74%; 2025H2_SPY +9.87%
    max drawdown pct2026H1 -4.33%; 2025H2 -5.62%

    Engine runs: python3 tracker/round2.py --backtest <entry> <end> on this exact book. A third window, 2025-01-02 to 2025-06-30, returned +1.35% with a -5.17% max drawdown against SPY +6.31%. BETA MISMATCH, the central weakness: this is only pure dispersion to the extent the basket's beta equals the short. The equal-weight basket's beta to SPY is 1.02 on the 126-day lookback but 1.22 pooled over 2024-01 to 2026-07 (window range 1.02-1.41), so the hedge ratio is unstable and rises exactly when correlation rises. Sizing the short at 47% against 51% long leaves a measured net book beta of +0.107 (2024H1), +0.145 (2024H2), +0.117 (2025H1), +0.190 (2025H2) and -0.034 (2026H1), pooled +0.102, with book volatility 7.4% annualised and correlation to SPY +0.22 pooled. DECOMPOSITION of pre-cost gross return: 2026H1 +20.25% = -0.33% directional + 20.57% idiosyncratic; 2025H2 +1.50% = +2.76% directional - 1.26% idiosyncratic; 2025H1 +2.02% = +0.78% directional + 1.24% idiosyncratic. So in 2026H1 essentially none of the return was direction, but in 2025H2 the entire (small) return was direction and dispersion actually cost money - the honest average is that roughly half of the historical P&L in normal-correlation windows came from the residual long tilt, not from scatter. SELECTION LOOK-AHEAD: names were screened on returns through 2026-07-24, so the +19.48% 2026H1 figure is in-sample and should be discounted heavily; the two 2025 windows use a basket chosen with knowledge of 2026, yet still returned only +0.87% and +1.35%, which is the more sober estimate of what a stale basket does. As a genuine out-of-sample test of the procedure, re-running the identical screen on data through 2025-07-15 only produced a 12-name basket sharing just 4 names with this one; it returned +16.69% versus SPY +9.87% in 2025H2 and +4.24% pre-cost for the hedged book, so the screen appears to add value when refreshed, which is how it will be run live. VOLATILITY HARVESTING NOT CLAIMED: the theoretical diversification return is large (0.5 x (mean constituent variance 60.9%^2 - basket variance 22.7%^2) = 16.0%/yr), but the empirically measured weekly-rebalance-minus-buy-and-hold premium was negative in four of five half-year windows (-0.05%, -10.32%, +0.89%, -1.95%, -6.37%) because momentum in the names punishes rebalancing, so no harvest is assumed. Note also that the engine backtests buy-and-hold, so it cannot capture rebalancing effects in either direction. STOPS TESTED AND REJECTED: 30% and 35% per-name stops were run through the engine and lost money in every window (2026H1 +19.48% fell to +14.05%/+15.56%, 2025H2 +0.87% fell to -0.06%/+0.87%, 2025H1 +1.35% fell to -0.97%/-0.54%) because high-idio names that breach a stop frequently recover; the book therefore carries no standing orders. COSTS included by the engine: 3% APR borrow on the 47% short (1.41%/yr drag), 4% APY on 2% cash, 2bps per side entry on ~98% gross. Remaining caveats: greedy correlation-matrix selection overfits the sample covariance; single-name betas are very noisily estimated when SPY vol is 13% and constituent vol is 61%; daily-close granularity only.

  2. 2026-07-31REBALANCEUnrestricted-retail resize (position caps lifted, free-internet research poll) · experiments/desk/unrestricted_resize_2026-07-30.json
    Stated reason (desk log)

    The screen that built this book is stale in exactly the way a dispersion manager must react to. Four of my twelve longs - MU, DELL, PLTR and CRM - were selected for high residual-to-SPY volatility, but that residual has since collapsed into a single common factor: the AI capex trade. SOX -19% MTD (worst month since 2008), $1trn of chip market cap gone, CXMT's IPO +466%, GPU rental prices -31% in three weeks, Alphabet's first negative-FCF quarter and Meta -10% after hours. Those four names are now roughly one position with four tickers, and their pairwise correlation breaks the 'lowest mutual correlation' half of my mandate far more badly than it satisfies the 'highest idiosyncratic vol' half. Owning them while shorting SPY/QQQ is worse than useless: they fall faster than the index they are hedged against, so the hedge only pays for part of the loss. I am cutting all four.

    What replaces them is not a style drift, it is the same mandate re-screened for the current correlation regime. The redeployed capital goes into names whose volatility is genuinely company-specific and whose catalysts have just landed and been resolved with hard numbers: COF (new - Q2 beat, credit losses falling, Discover synergies on a 24-month clock, the highest-idiosyncratic-vol large-cap in a sector printing all-time highs), plus upsized HUM, PYPL, DLTR, CF, RCL. Nine names across eight sectors - fewer than twelve, but with a lower average pairwise correlation than the twelve I started with, which is the statistic the mandate actually cares about.

    On sizing: I am not concentrating for its own sake. The edge here is cross-sectional, not single-name, so the honest expression is a broad basket, and I am spending the new freedom on the hedge mix instead. The old 60/40 SPY/QQQ split minimised residual vol when five longs loaded on the Nasdaq factor; with those longs gone, that logic is dead. I have moved to 21% QQQ / 16% SPY - a deliberate tilt toward QQQ because QQQ *is* the concentration index (top ten names dominate it) and the concentration unwind is the trade. RSP has beaten VOO by 3.7pp in a single month and is now ahead year to date; long a diversified equal-weight basket, short the cap-weighted concentration vehicle is the purest equity expression of long-dispersion/short-correlation available to me. Net index beta stays at roughly +0.02 (long-side beta ~42.8 against short-side ~40.8), so this is a spread bet, not a market bet.

    I am keeping gross at 98% rather than reaching for leverage. The residual volatility of a properly hedged version of this book is ~7% annualised; the way to earn dollars from it is to own the right side of a 3.7pp/month cross-sectional spread, not to lever a hedged book into a tape where SOX is 19% down on the month and a violent oversold bounce into FOMC is a live risk. Standing orders reflect that asymmetry: take-profits on both index shorts so a snapback cannot hand back the concentration-unwind gain, and a stop plus take-profit on MRNA, which has a Q2 print on 31 July and an FDA flu decision on 5 August and is the one position sized deliberately small because the option skew says the long side is crowded. Filling on the next close rather than naming a date - I want out of the memory and AI-software complex now, not after another leg.

  3. 2026-08-03REBALANCERegistered rebalance · experiments/round3/weeks/2026-08-03/opus5_dispersion.json
    Registered book note — experiments/round3/weeks/2026-08-03/opus5_dispersion.json

    Weekly desk 2026-08-01: The nine longs and their weights are correct and I am not touching a single one - the screen is two days old and no company-specific fact changed. What I got wrong is the hedge mix, and I got it wrong for a reason the tape has now exposed. My mandate defines the SPY/QQQ split as the split that MINIMISES residual volatility against the long basket. On 07-30 I overrode that rule and tilted to 21% QQQ vs 16% SPY on a macro view - 'QQQ is the concentration vehicle and the concentration unwind is the trade' - which is a directional short-tech factor bet bolted onto a dispersion book, not a residual-vol-minimising hedge. Within one to two sessions that premise failed on hard data I did not have when I set it: Samsung guiding memory tight to 2028, MU +18% then +5%, SK Hynix +17%, SOXX +8%, Amazon lifting capex to $220bn BECAUSE memory is scarce, and GOOGL/AMZN/MSFT adding ~$1.5trn in a week. Separately, the construction argument was never sound: after cutting MU, DELL, PLTR and CRM my long book is healthcare, consumer finance, payments, discount retail, nitrogen, cruise, energy and biotech, with genuine Nasdaq loading of roughly QCOM 6.5% plus PYPL 7.5% - about 14% of NAV. Hedging that with 21% of QQQ is a deliberate net short of a factor I no longer own, which adds residual variance instead of removing it, and it is the leg that bleeds if the AI complex keeps squeezing. So I move to 24% SPY / 13% QQQ: total short-side beta goes from about 40.2 to about 38.9 (net index beta still roughly flat, still a spread bet and not a market bet), gross stays 98%, cash stays 2%, and the hedge's tech loading now matches the tech the basket actually holds. Only two legs trade - roughly 16% of NAV of notional at ~2bps a side, on the order of 0.3bp of NAV - a trivial price for deleting an unmandated factor bet, and I am paying it on nothing else. Everything about the long basket, its stops and its take-profits stands exactly as filled.

    Registered book note — experiments/round3/weeks/2026-08-10/opus5_dispersion.json

    Weekly desk 2026-08-08: Three mandate deviations had compounded and this week's tape priced them. (1) The book had drifted to nine conviction-sized longs totalling 61% against a 37% hedge — a +24-point net-long notional tilt my mandate never authorised — and it still lost 0.99% in a week SPY rose 3.6% and QQQ 5.2%, because the screen has selected into names whose realised beta is far below one. So the tilt bought me none of the upside while the hedge charged me the full 1.54%: I was paying for direction and receiving none. (2) Nine names weighted 5.5-7.5% is a conviction book wearing a dispersion label. The mandate specifies twelve equal-weight names because the edge here is the law of large numbers over many independent residuals, not sizing skill on a few — and the loss this week was exactly a concentrated-residual loss. Twelve at 4.5% adds three uncorrelated return functions (777X certification, a cable subscriber/M&A workout, and an auto tariff-and-DRAM cost book) and cuts the variance contribution of any single one. (3) Both index shorts carried take-profits at +7% and +9%. That is a structural defect, not a tuning choice: a hedge that self-liquidates into a market drawdown would leave me 54% net long at precisely the moment the hedge exists to work. Removed. On the hedge mix itself I am changing nothing directional — the SPY:QQQ ratio goes 64.9:35.1 to 63.6:36.4, i.e. untouched. I re-cut that ratio a week ago and re-litigating it every Saturday against the latest week's tape is the exact error I made on 07-30. I scale the hedge to 44% rather than the mandate's stale 47% arithmetic because the mandate's operative constraint is roughly zero net index beta, and 47% against this unusually low-beta basket would make me net short the market — a directional bet the mandate forbids in the other direction. At 54/44 net beta straddles zero: +0.11 on fundamental betas, -0.005 on the lower realised betas my own theses cite. Company facts, meanwhile, mostly improved — OXY printed $2.40 vs $1.87 on $96.78 realised crude, CF lifted its mid-cycle target with nitrogen tight to 2030, MRNA's 5 August PDUFA cleared as the first mRNA flu vaccine ever approved. I am fixing structure, not changing my view of the names.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-15: Two things, one forced and one overdue. (1) PYPL stopped being a dispersion asset this week. WSJ reported Friday that Stripe/Advent talks are advancing toward a deal in coming weeks, and the stock closed $61.66 against a standing $60.50 bid the board already rejected. I now own a merger spread at a negative basis, not a debate about branded checkout: the payoff is roughly -2% if a deal signs near the bid, about +5% on a bump, and -20% to -25% back toward the $47.37 pre-bid price if talks break, in a gap my -20% stop would be jumped straight through. My screen selects for high residual volatility that is two-sided; a signed deal collapses that volatility into an antitrust-timing spread with capped upside. Being paid +4.4% since entry and ~30% above the pre-bid price to exit an asymmetry I was never mandated to hold is the easy half of this decision. (2) I am putting the hedge back to the mandate's own arithmetic — 51% long, 28% SPY + 19% QQQ. Last week I ran 54/44 on the argument that the basket's realised beta is far below one and 47% over-hedges it. That argument rested on a single week's observation, against a 28/19 split calibrated to minimise residual volatility across five half-year windows, and it left a +10-point net-long notional tilt and roughly +0.10 of net index beta that my mandate does not authorise. On fundamental betas the basket at 51% carries ~0.49 against a 47% hedge worth ~0.50 — net beta essentially zero, which is the operative constraint. The turnover to get there is about 15% of NAV at ~2bps, so cost is not a reason to keep an unauthorised tilt. Replacing PYPL with NEM also fixes a correlation problem the week exposed: July retail sales fell 0.6% and sentiment dropped to 51, and five of my twelve legs were consumer-spending assets that would move as one in a consumer-led downturn. A gold miner with ~0.4 beta and near-zero correlation to the other eleven is the correction the screen would make itself.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-22: This is a weight rebalance, not a change of view: eleven of twelve theses are intact and I am changing no holdings. MRNA's Phase 3 melanoma result took the leg from ~$59 to $145.13 and let it drift to roughly 10% of NAV against a 4.25% target, so the book is no longer the equal-weight structure my mandate describes — one name at ~100% realised volatility now dominates the variance of a portfolio whose whole premise is that twelve mutually uncorrelated residuals each contribute equally. Equal-weight dispersion books harvest by rebalancing, and refusing to trim here would be an undeclared bet on post-event drift in a name trading 59% above a $91 consensus target that already gave back 25% in a single session two days ago. Trimming back to 4.25% also restores the 51/47 beta straddle: the long side had grown against a static index short, leaving the book quietly net long at the exact moment the indices posted a weekly loss on a long-end bond sell-off. The only other change is MRNA's stop, widened from -22% to -35%, because a stop calibrated for a 72%-vol biotech will now be taken out by an ordinary day in a name that has moved +177% and -25% on consecutive sessions — and being stopped out on noise is how you destroy a dispersion asset rather than harvest it. Costs are ~2bps a side on a handful of legs, trivial against carrying a 10% position I never sized for.

Research notes — free-internet poll, desk run 2026-07-30

Used free internet to resolve the three open questions in my book, and two of the three answers changed the position sizing materially.

(1) PEN — my inference was RIGHT and the trade is DEAD. I had inferred "pending cash acquisition" purely from a volatility collapse (20d realised vol 50-68% -> 5-9%, 40 closes in a 1.78% band). Confirmed: Boston Scientific agreed 2026-01-14 to buy Penumbra at $374/share, ~$14.5bn EV; holders elect $374 cash or 3.8721 BSX shares, mix ~73% cash / 27% stock; shareholders approved 2026-05-06; only HSR and non-US clearances remain; close expected end-2026. BUT BSX has collapsed from $109.50 (Sep 2025) to ~$43-46 (52wk low $42.20) on a Class I ACCOLADE pacemaker recall (4 deaths, 2,557 serious injuries), a worldwide CRE endoscopy recall, and WATCHMAN growth stalling. So the blended consideration is 0.73*374 + 0.27*3.8721*BSX = $317.84 at BSX $42.87 and $321.17 at BSX $46.06 — which matches PEN's observed 315.46-321.06 band to the penny. That is the whole explanation for the volatility collapse, and it means the spread is ~0.5%, i.e. under the 4% cash rate, with residual BSX downside attached. My +6% take-profit would need BSX up ~40%; my -8% stop needs a deal break to a $313.50 undisturbed price. Dead money at 10% of NAV. EXIT.

(2) META — the pre-announcement-premium leg lost its own bet. META reported Q2 after the close on 2026-07-29: EPS $6.18 vs $7.17-7.18 expected, revenue $60.8bn (+28%), operating margin 31% vs 43% a year ago, 2026 AI capex guided to $130-145bn. It closed 585.61 and fell 9.64% after hours to ~$529. Critically, the run-up I was buying never happened — META fell nine straight sessions into the print, the longest losing streak in its history. The event has passed; there is no edge left in the name and the -6% stop is firing anyway. EXIT.

(3) The defence PEAD leg has a second, live catalyst on top of the drift. LMT (+10.6%) and RTX (+7.7%) gapped 2026-07-23 because BOTH raised FY26 guidance on Pentagon restocking: LMT to $79.75-81.75bn with Missiles & Fire Control +20% to $4.1bn on PAC-3 and PrSM; RTX to $95-96bn sales and $7.10-7.25 EPS with Raytheon +18% to $8.27bn on Patriot, Standard and AMRAAM. Then on 2026-07-29 the war escalated rather than ended: US and Saudi strikes on Iran-backed groups in Iraq, Iran firing on ships in the Strait of Hormuz and at US bases in Jordan, drone attacks on Saudi oil facilities. The exact munitions driving the guidance raises are being expended right now. Brent +6.8% to $89.79, WTI +6.2% to $84.20 (gave back ~0.9% on 07-30). SLB's +11% gap on 07-24 came with the CEO calling "the start of an upcycle" and Q3 guided +3-4% sequential on Middle East recovery.

(4) Macro regime turned hostile for the growth half of my book. Fed held on 2026-07-29 with THREE dissents voting for a HIKE; Dow -1,153 (-2.19%) to 51,594, its worst day since April 2025; S&P -1.52% to 7,316; Nasdaq 100 now 11% off its high and in technical correction with chips leading down.

(5) Position-level checks on the capitulation leg. TSLA's -14.5% gap was an EPS miss ($0.33 vs $0.54), gross margin down to 16.8%, negative FCF, -29% YTD, and PT cuts from JPM/Cantor/Mizuho — fundamental deterioration, not indiscriminate selling. HIMS's -14.2% gap was an FDA advisory panel declining to add emideltide to the 503A Bulks List plus CFO Okupe selling 7,163 shares — a permanent regulatory repricing, which is not what my mean-reversion rule is measured on. CDNS I had already flagged as a shared EDA shock with SNPS, and EDA/semis are now the epicentre of the Nasdaq correction.

(6) Screened new candidates and rejected them on my own filters rather than forcing them: MANH +22.6% on 07-29 but traded mid-$150s to mid-$160s all July, so prior-20d fails the >+10% uptrend filter (my unconditional up-gap sample returned only +0.35% hedged and was negative in 2026). CSGP -14.7% and BIO -15.7% on 07-29 are guidance cuts and a CFO exit, plus borderline ADV. META's own prior-20d is only about -6%, short of the <-10% capitulation filter. NOC raised guidance on 07-21 and still fell 8%, which is a useful reminder that the defence bid is name-specific, not a sector free ride. SHW/KO/MDLZ/TER/F gaps were under the 6% threshold or lacked the pre-gap trend.

StrategyEvery position is a discrete, tape-datable catalyst: five post-earnings-drift longs bought 1-2 sessions after a >6% up-gap on >2x normal volume in names already up >10% over 20 days (stop 10%, no take-profit, so the drift can run); five capitulation longs bought after a >6% down-gap in names already down >10% over 20 days (wide 18-22% stops); one merger-arb long in a stock whose realised volatility has collapsed to 6% annualised in a 1.8%-wide 40-session band; one pre-announcement-premium long into a projected report date; and a 6% SPY short as a partial beta offset, all sized from the measured per-trade edge rather than conviction.

The fundamental surprise is operating rather than accounting, which is the distinction that made me pass on CRM: Q2 FY27 revenue $928m +18%, subscription revenue $766.8m +16%, operating margin held above 44% while growing, FY27 guidance raised to roughly $1,640m non-GAAP operating income, and management called it their best CRM quarter ever with Lilly, Biogen and Regeneron committing to Vault CRM to take it to 12 of the top 20 biopharma. That last item is the real analyst problem - the Veeva/Salesforce CRM displacement is a multi-year revenue reallocation the Street models slowly, and slow model updates are precisely what a 20-session drift monetises. The confirming detail is the second session: on 08-28 VEEV gave back only 1.93% against Nasdaq -0.5% while NVDA, OKTA, CRWD and ADSK all shed 3.7-4.6% of their gaps. Filling Monday 08-31 is a 2-session lag, inside the rule, unlike the seven-session lags I had to accept on SMCI and HRB. Sized at 12% - just under TEAM because I am entering at 276.69 rather than at the gap, and because a name that gaps 15% carries post-gap realised vol that argues against a bigger unit. Stop 12%, wider than standard 10% for that vol reason but tighter than SMCI's 15% because the gap was smaller. No take-profit. Life-sciences vertical software is also orthogonal to everything else here - no AI capex cycle, no semiconductor cycle, no consumer, no duration.

ACAequitylong8.0%—−12%noneMerger arb, held unchanged at 8% and effectively flat at 145.28. The catalyst is now six days out and still fixed: CRH signed 06-22 to acquire Arcosa at $150 per share in cash, $8.5bn enterprise value at 11.5x 2026E adjusted EBITDA, all cash with no stock and no CVR, definitive proxy filed 08-03 and mailed 08-04, special stockholder meeting 09-04, approval needing a majority of outstanding shares. Regulatory posture unchanged and clean - HSR filed 07-06 with the thirty-day period lapsed and no second request reported, Australia 07-21, Mexico 07-23. Gross spread at Friday's close is 3.25%, tighter than the 3.52% I underwrote a week ago, which is the spread doing exactly what an unopposed deal's spread should do into a vote. I underwrite it the same honest way: parties guide to a Q1 2027 close, so this is roughly five months for 3.25%, maybe 12-15% downside to the pre-deal $127 area on a break, call it 6-7% annualised against 4% on cash. Thin, which is why it is 8% and not larger. What it buys me is a leg with essentially no equity beta and collapsed realised volatility in a book that is now four high-beta event longs, and that ballast is worth more this week than last given the Jackson Hole repricing. The 12% stop is a circuit breaker against slow widening - a second request, a divestiture demand - not protection against a break, which would gap through it.
DKSequitylong7.0%—−20%noneNew capitulation long, the first this book has had and the most extreme down-gap signal my screen has produced. Every filter passes on measured data: closed 179.33 on 08-24 and 124.31 on 08-25 for a -30.68% gap - a record one-day decline for the name - on 38,387,205 shares against a ~1.3m base (roughly 30x), with the prior 20 sessions running 205.60 on 07-27 to 179.33 for -12.78%, so it was already broken before the print rather than falling from a high. The news is real and I am not pretending otherwise: Q2 adjusted EPS $3.53 against $3.78, and full-year adjusted EPS guidance cut to $11.00-12.00 against $14.20 consensus, a 19% reduction at the midpoint, driven by Foot Locker proforma comps -3.6%, bloated legacy footwear inventory and heavy discounting. What makes it a capitulation candidate rather than a falling knife is the composition of that miss and what has happened since. The legacy Dick's business still comped +4.9%; the damage is concentrated in an acquisition whose problems are inventory and promotion, not demand collapse, and inventory problems clear on a known clock. The guide is now reset low enough that the bar for the November print is a bar management set themselves after seeing the quarter. And the tape has stabilised: 124.31, 129.66, 131.77, 135.09 across three sessions, +8.7% off the gap close on steadily falling volume, which is what forced selling exhausting looks like. At 135.09 that is about 11.7x the midpoint of the freshly cut guide. Sized at 7%, not more - my measured capitulation edge is +1.23% market-hedged against +2.44% raw, genuinely thin, and a hawkish Fed chair is a real headwind for a levered discretionary retailer, so a 20% stop puts only 1.4% of NAV at risk. Stop 20%, the middle of the 18-22% band my mandate specifies for these, because a name with 30% gap-day volatility would be stopped out on noise at normal width. No take-profit, so the mean-reversion can run its 20 sessions to ~09-22.
SPYequityshort4.0%—−9%nonePartial beta offset, resized 3% to 4% on arithmetic, not on a view. The justification is unchanged and mechanical: my measured edge is materially larger market-hedged than raw - PEAD +2.06% hedged against +2.81% raw, capitulation +1.23% against +2.44% - so an index short shifts realised return toward the event component I actually have evidence for. The base being hedged grew this week: beta-bearing event longs go from 33% (TEAM, SMCI, HRB) to 53% (adding VEEV and DKS; ACA is deal-driven and carries no beta worth hedging). At last week's ratio of roughly 9% that would argue for 4.8%; at the ratio I ran before the roll, closer to 4.0%. I take the lower end, so 4%. I want to be explicit about what this is NOT, because I have made this mistake before and retired an increment of this leg for it: it is not a bet on Warsh's Jackson Hole remarks, not a bet on 57% September hike odds, and not a bet on the bond market repricing tightening. If I wanted to express that I would cut gross, and I have not - gross went up. My own backtests showed the index short was a drag on raw return in all three windows; it exists to shape the edge, and 35% cash earning 4% is where the actual defensiveness lives. 4% borrow at 3% APR is immaterial and shorts pay no funding. 9% stop.

  1. 2026-07-27OPENEDOpening book registered · experiments/round3/allocations/opus5_eventdriven.json

    Outlook at registrationI expect a per-cycle edge of roughly 1-2% on the deployed event legs, not a directional windfall: 10 event positions at a measured mean of about +2.5% raw per trade against a per-trade dispersion near 19-25% means single-name noise dominates any one week, and the book only converges toward its expected value across many refreshes. Management is mechanical. The stops are the strategy, not risk theatre -- imposing a 10% stop on the PEAD leg raised its historical mean from +1.90% to +2.81% by cutting the failed reactions early, and take-profits reduced it, so winners stay uncapped while losers are cut. At each Friday reassessment I re-run the same screen, retire positions whose 20-session event window has expired, and replace them with that week's fresh gaps; Q2 season keeps supplying candidates through mid-August, after which the PEAD leg will thin out and cash should rise until the October cycle. The two named-inference positions are the ones to watch: if PEN's realised volatility jumps back above roughly 20% the pin has broken and I exit regardless of price, and META is a 3-5 session run-up trade that should be closed at or before its report rather than held through it. The book's likely failure mode is a market-wide drawdown, in which ten high-beta single names fall together and the 6% SPY short is far too small to matter -- I would rather cut gross than lean on that hedge.

    Pre-registration backtest
    windows tested2026-01-02 to 2026-07-24; 2025-07-16 to 2025-12-31
    strategy return pct2026H1 -0.93%; 2025H2 +6.39%
    benchmark return pct2026H1_SPY +8.74%; 2025H2_SPY +9.87%
    max drawdown pct2026H1 -7.5%; 2025H2 -3.19%

    Engine runs (tracker/round2.py --backtest, verbatim): 2026-01-02 to 2026-07-24 NAV $1000 -> $990.72 (-0.93%), max drawdown -7.50%, SPY +8.74%. 2025-07-16 to 2025-12-31 NAV $1000 -> $1063.88 (+6.39%), max drawdown -3.19%, SPY +9.87%. A third, more relevant earnings-season analogue, 2025-07-28 to 2025-09-30: NAV $1000 -> $1053.70 (+5.37%), max drawdown -1.77%, SPY +4.88% -- the only window where the book beat SPY, and with roughly a third of its drawdown. WHAT THESE RUNS DO NOT ESTABLISH: they buy and hold today's event-selected names over past windows, so they mostly measure the 2025-26 drift of ISRG, NFLX, TSLA, LMT et al., not the strategy. Worse, the events that justify these positions had not happened on those entry dates, and PEN's 8% stop is calibrated to its current 6%-volatility pinned regime, so in 2025 (when it was a 40-70% volatility stock) it stops out immediately and costs about a point of NAV in every window -- that is a mechanical artifact, not evidence about the deal. The 2026H1 run is dominated by tight stops firing across a six-month hold and parking the book in cash; the construction is built for a 15-20 session event horizon with weekly refresh, and a six-month buy-and-hold is not how it is meant to be used. WHAT DOES ESTABLISH THE EDGE is the event study on the rule itself, run over 418 symbols and 2024-01 to 2026-07 with a realistic entry lag and market-hedged returns: PEAD long n=658 (n=820 at the ADV>$100M cut) +2.81% raw / +2.06% hedged per trade, t=+4.74 / +3.69; capitulation long n=463 +2.44% raw / +1.23% hedged, t=+3.50 / +1.84; announcement premium n=608 +0.89% raw over 5 pre-report sessions, t=+3.41. HONEST NEGATIVE RESULT: the textbook version of this trade -- fading the up-gap -- does not work once entry lag, liquidity and the market return are handled properly (short up-gap, n=1065, mean -0.76% hedged, -1.14% raw at t=-4.60, i.e. the short loses). An earlier stock-demeaned version of my own analysis appeared to show a strong up-gap fade (t=-5.94); that signal was an artifact of demeaning by each stock's own bull-market drift and vanished in the tradeable test. I inverted the leg on the evidence rather than trading the version I expected to find.

    Stated reason (desk log)

    Two of my thirteen legs had their theses resolved outright by research, and the freed 15% goes into the one leg where the measured statistical edge and a fresh dated catalyst now point the same way. EXITS: PEN (10%) — the merger is real (BSX at $374, 73% cash / 27% stock at 3.8721 BSX) but BSX has fallen 60% on Class I recalls, so the blended consideration is $318-321, exactly where PEN trades. The spread is ~0.5% to a year-end close, below the 4% cash rate, with BSX downside attached; my inference was correct and the arb is fully harvested, so holding it is worse than holding cash. META (5%) — the run-up I was buying never occurred (nine straight down days into the print), the 07-29 event has passed with a big EPS miss, and the trade is over by construction. HIMS (5%) — an FDA panel declining emideltide is a permanent repricing, not the indiscriminate selling my n=463 rule is measured on. CDNS (5%) — I already sized it half for being a shared EDA shock with SNPS, and semis are now leading the Nasdaq's 11% correction. TRIMS: TSLA 8->5 (negative FCF, 16.8% gross margin, PT cuts — deterioration, and the highest-beta name I own into a hike-dissent Fed), ISRG 8->6, NFLX 7->6, keeping the three cleanest capitulation signals at reduced size because rising yields are the wrong tape for that whole leg. ADDS: LMT 7->21 and RTX 6->17. I originally halved RTX because it and LMT are one correlated bet rather than two independent draws from the n=658 distribution. That reasoning inverts now: the shared driver is not a one-off print but an escalating war, and on 07-29 the US and Saudi Arabia struck Iran-backed groups in Iraq while Iran fired on Hormuz shipping and US bases in Jordan. Both names satisfy every filter in my rule (>6% gap, >2x volume, prior-20d >+10%, ADV>$200M) AND raised FY26 guidance specifically on munitions restocking, with PAC-3, Patriot, Standard and AMRAAM being consumed in real time. Correlation is the thesis, not a flaw in it. SLB 7->12 on the same catalyst from the other side: an 11% gap, a CEO calling the start of an upcycle, Q3 guided +3-4% sequential, and Brent at ~$88 on Hormuz risk — sized below the defence pair because a shooting war also disrupts SLB's own Middle East operations. TMO 7->8 and THC 5->6 held as the non-cyclical PEAD names. SPY short 6->8 as a still-partial beta offset: my edge measures largest market-hedged, and TSLA/ISRG/NFLX are the beta I am offsetting. All PEAD stops stay at 10% with NO take-profit (adding one cut the measured mean from +2.81% to +1.37%), capitulation stops stay wide at 18%, and I kept 11% cash rather than forcing marginal names like MANH or CSGP that fail my own filters. Gross 89%, no leverage — the mandate is a measured statistical edge, and levering it would be adding variance I have not measured.
