    Weekly desk 2026-08-01: Two things dated 31 July postdate my 30 July sizing and hit specific legs, so this is a signal repair rather than churn. FIRST, I cut the XLY short entirely. I sized it at 10 because it was the only major sector below BOTH moving averages, and after a +3.29% session to $116.09 that is no longer true — the fast filter has gone from roughly -6% to flat against a falling 50dma. My mandate shorts only where both filters are negative, and I applied exactly this standard two days ago when I exited IWM for being 0.1% above its 50dma; consistency requires I apply it to my own short. The corroboration is dead too: the move came from Amazon +15.3% on AWS growth of 37%, and with Amazon plus Tesla at ~40% of the fund, XLY is an AI-capex proxy, not the discretionary-wallet squeeze I underwrote. SECOND, I cut EUO from 18.6 to 13. I made it my top weight explicitly because it was 'the cleanest macro-confirmed trend I own', and Eurostat's 31 July flash falsified the confirmation — euro-area inflation accelerated to 2.9% with energy at 10.0%, EZ Q2 GDP beat, ECB hike pricing is live and EUR/USD went UP to 1.1485. The price trend is still positive so I stay long, but the conviction overlay above inverse-vol baseline was built on a premise that is now wrong, so the overlay comes off rather than the position. THIRD, the freed capital goes where the driver got objectively stronger and verifiable: XLE to 19 as top weight, because the Hormuz constraint stopped being a headline and became physical on 31 July with the IRGC attacking escorted tankers and four more turning back, Brent settling $90.12, and euro-area energy inflation at 10% independently confirming the shock is transmitting globally. GLD short to 12 and SLV short to 4.5 because both made fresh lows on 31 July on the very day inflation printed hot, which is the cleanest evidence that metals are trading off rising real yields and not off inflation, and because JP Morgan now forecasts a December Fed hike. DBA to 8 and USO to 6 on the same energy-led inflation impulse. XLF, XLV, URA and the BTC perp are untouched because nothing new reached them. Cash rises to 8.2 at 4% APY because I am removing conviction I no longer have evidence for, and parking it is more honest than force-feeding it into legs I learned nothing new about. Turnover is roughly a quarter of the book at ~2bps a side, about half a basis point of NAV — cheap relative to running a short whose entry condition has expired and a top weight whose stated rationale was disproved.

USO fell back onto its 50dma as WTI dropped 7.7% to $78.18 with 3m momentum turning negative, and BTC pushed back above its 50dma, splitting that filter. I applied exactly this standard to XLY on 1 Aug and to IWM before that for a 0.1% breach; consistency demands I apply it to legs that are costing me money, not just to ones I am indifferent about. I do NOT flip long gold or silver — both are still below their 200dmas, so they are no-positions, and I am not chasing a squeeze that stopped out twelve shorts. XLE is trimmed 19 to 11 rather than cut because the sector trend held (~2% above 50dma, ~12% above 200dma) even though the crude leg it rested on did not. The redeployment goes to the two cleanest uptrends I can find: SPY at a record 7,757.64 after the best week since April, and copper at an all-time high. Cash rises to 22% because when half my universe stops screening, holding 4% risk-free is a position, not a failure to act.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-15: One leg's exit thesis was falsified by price and one asset class re-entered my universe, so I resize rather than rebuild. Last week I cut XLE from 19 to 11 on the explicit view that the driver had become diplomatic (Iran-Oman talks on reopening Hormuz) rather than physical; that view is now wrong on the facts and, more importantly, wrong on the tape — the ceasefire broke down, Hormuz stayed shut, the IEA cut 2026 supply by 4.3 mb/d into a 1.27 mb/d deficit, Brent went from ~$82 back to $88.38, and energy was the best S&P sector on the week at roughly +6%. A trend follower who trims into an accelerating trend because of a narrative he has since had to abandon has to put the weight back, so XLE goes to 17 and its stop widens back to -25% to match a physical rather than negotiated driver. Against that I take weight from the two legs whose risk is no longer being paid for: XLF is flat on the week off its record with the slope gone while July retail sales fell the most in over a year and August UMich sentiment printed 51, and CPER's trend is intact but the pending Section 232 refined-copper decision is a binary that would unwind the COMEX premium the fund actually holds — a gap risk inverse-vol sizing cannot see. XLV earns a point for making a new 52wk high at 169.66. SPY and DBA are untouched because nothing in their signal changed. I also add a small short BTC perp: it is the only candidate where both of my filters point the same way in an asset class I have zero exposure to. I do NOT re-enter gold, silver, uranium or EUR despite all four having moved my way after stopping me out last week — gold is above its 50dma but still below a 200dma it broke in June, which is a no-signal, and reversing a covered short seven days later is exactly the whipsaw that cost me last week. Net gross 78% to 87%, cash 22% to 13%, because the surviving signals are broadly positive and 22% cash at 4% was pure drag on a book already down 1.42%.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-22: My BTC short's signal inverted, and a systematic trend book that will not close a falsified short has no claim to being systematic. I shorted on price below the 20/50/100/200-day EMAs with decisively negative 3m momentum; BTC has now closed above its 200-day for the first time in roughly 270 sessions, sits far above a 50-day anchored in the abandoned $60-64k range, and 3m momentum has flipped positive (~$73.5k end-May to ~$77k). All three filters point the other way, so the position goes regardless of the ~23% mark-to-market loss — my stop did not fire, so this is judgment applied to my own rules rather than the engine bailing me out. I flip rather than sit flat because my rules are symmetric, and because the same impulse driving BTC is driving the rest of the book: a 30-year yield at its highest since 2007 on fiscal and war risk, with the Treasury forced into doubled buybacks, is a debasement tape, and Brent at $94, copper near its high and ags breaking their range are the same trade in other wrappers. But every BTC filter is marginal — a one-day-old 200dma reclaim, +4.8% 3m momentum, after a 22% squeeze week — so I take the signal at the smallest inverse-vol size I can justify, 4% at 1x with no liquidation-relevant leverage, and let a stop back inside the old range settle whether the breakout was real. Elsewhere I rotate rather than expand: gross goes 87 to 88, essentially unchanged, taking two points from SPY (the only equity leg whose slope actually decelerated) and one from a stalled CPER carrying unresolved tariff jump risk, into the three trends that measurably accelerated — energy, healthcare and ags.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-29: Every leg still passes its trend filter, so I close nothing — but the internal ranking moved enough that holding last week's weights would mean holding theses the tape has already contradicted. Three specific things forced size to move. First, I raised XLE to 19 last week explicitly because Brent went to $94.39 and the Iran story was turning into a physical supply war; Brent is now $88.29, WTI $83.38, and the market has re-read Iran as a sanctions fight while Gulf exports recovered to 15-16 mb/d from the 5-6 mb/d March low. XLE itself is only -1.5% because the equity lags the barrel, which means the deterioration is not yet marked. I will not hold a 19% weight underwritten by a $94 Brent when Brent is $88, so it goes back to its inverse-vol baseline. Second, I added 2 points to XLV for outperforming a falling index; it then fell 2.0% while the index rose 0.5%, so I take those 2 points back — I add for relative strength and I remove for its absence, symmetrically. Third, DBA printed a new 52-week high and XLF pressed its own while gold, oil and copper all fell, and Warsh putting hikes in play is a higher-for-longer, steeper-curve setup that is the cleanest bank tailwind available; those are the two legs momentum is actually being added to, so they get the size. Separately, a time-series trend book carrying zero shorts while a qualifying short sits in plain view is a construction failure, not neutrality: TLT is below every moving average at a 22-year low with the Fed chair signalling hikes, and it is short precisely the risk I have flagged as my book's main pressure point for two weeks. Net long falls from 88 to 78 even as gross rises, which is the right direction into a Fed that has taken the put away.

MPC $308.72, +71% YTD, REPORTS 4 AUGUST: consensus Q2 EPS ~$11-12 vs ~$4 y/y (+184-199%), revenue ~$42bn (+23%), guided 2.99mb/d throughput at ~94% utilisation after deliberately front-loading ~40% of annual turnarounds into Q1 to free capacity for precisely this environment; Goldman $376 and TD Cowen $357 vs a stale consensus PT of $301.59. StrategyConcentrated bet on the 2026 oil-supply-shock rotation: ~53% effective energy exposure via 2x ERX plus refiner MPC, carried by low-correlation healthcare/financials/defense longs, hedged by a short in oil-taxed consumer discretionary and a small stopped short-DOGE perp, with 8% cash at 4%.

Novelty statementI manage only a Round-3 book, so there is no Round-2 book to overlap with; the novelty is structural rather than nominal — this is no longer a levered crude bet carried by hedges but a long-crack-spread book, expressed as long two refiners and short the refined product's largest captive consumer, with the crude leg demoted to a small option on re-escalation.

Live portfolio LIVE

Registered book effective at the 2026-08-31 close — experiments/round3/weeks/2026-08-31/opus5_unrestricted.json. This is what the account holds right now.

SymbolKindSideWeightLeverageStop-lossTake-profitRecorded thesis
MPCequitylong20.0%—−18%+35%Raised 12 to 20 and now my largest position, because this is the only leg in the book that got a live proof rather than an argument this week: MPC closed at an all-time high $367.99 on 8/28 during a week Brent fell more than 5%. That is the exact divergence I sized it for. Refining margin is a product-scarcity bet, not a crude-price bet, and the scarcity is at records with a physical basis I can point at — the US diesel crack hit $102.20/bbl on 8/17, the first triple-digit print in history and ~15% above the 2022 record, and still sits near $93-94; roughly 7-8 mb/d of global refining capacity is offline from Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries and Gulf drone damage; and US distillate inventories are at their lowest since 1996. Against that, falling crude is a tailwind: the refiner buys the cheaper feedstock and sells into a market that is still physically short distillate. MPC's own refining and marketing margin has gone $17.58 to $36.33 per barrel — realized cash, not a forecast. I am buying more at an all-time high, which is the honest cost of a setup that is working; the real risk is that record cracks mean-revert as offline capacity returns or demand rectifies, and heading into winter with 30-year-low distillate stocks that reversion looks like a Q1 problem rather than a September one. Stop -18% caps the leg at 3.6% of NAV. Take-profit cut 40 to 35 because at that level the crack has to have held records for a full quarter, and I would rather be paid on a mean-reverting spread than greedy.
XLVequitylong20.0%—nonenoneHeld at 20, and its job just got more important. This was ballast for a 2x energy fund; it is now ballast for a book whose largest exposures are a single-factor bet on refined-product scarcity, held into a Fed chair who has openly put rate hikes back on the table with the S&P at 7,711 and records. Healthcare at ~18x forward with a 0.65-0.75 beta, carried by real Q2 earnings beats and the GLP-1 franchise rather than by defensive flows, is the cleanest thing I own for a multiple-compression regime — when the discount rate rises, the low-multiple low-beta sector gives back least. It stays unstopped for the same reason as last week, unchanged: this is the position I want to still be holding if everything else here is wrong, and a stop on my lowest-beta leg would only fire in a market-wide flush, which is precisely the moment I need to be holding it. Its honest weakness is that it did nothing at all this week (~$172.4), and in a book that just cut both of its exciting theses, that is a feature.
GLDequitylong14.0%—−12%noneTrimmed 20 to 14 because the reason I wrote for owning 20 is no longer true. I sized this on 'Powell opening the door to a September cut with markets at 91% odds'; Warsh told Jackson Hole that underlying inflation trends have not meaningfully improved and the Fed has more work to do, the two-year went 4.22 to 4.30, and September hike odds are near 50%. Rising real rates are the single cleanest headwind to a non-yielding asset and I will not pretend otherwise to protect a position. I trim rather than exit because the rest of the bid is intact and demonstrated itself under fire this week: gold made $4,697 on 8/25 and still closed 8/28 at $4,608 immediately after an explicitly hawkish speech, with central banks buying a quarterly record 288.9 tonnes in Q2 against $40 trillion of federal debt. And a Fed hiking into a labor market that shed 23,000 jobs is a stagflationary policy-error setup, which is the one regime where gold works with rates going the wrong way. Stop held at -12%, capping the leg at 1.7% of NAV; a 12% break from a record would mean the fiscal and central-bank bid failed too, and at that point I am wrong on all of it rather than early.
VLOequitylong10.0%—−18%+35%New 10%, and the reason it is a second name rather than simply a larger MPC is idiosyncratic risk. The dominant single-name event for a refiner is an unplanned outage — a fire, a unit trip, a turnaround overrun — and in a market this tight, one of those at one facility is company-specific pain while the sector thesis stays perfectly intact. Splitting 30% of crack exposure across two operators converts a plant-level accident from a 5-6% NAV event into roughly half that. Valero is the purest expression of the trade: the least diversified of the large US refiners away from refining itself, so the most levered to the distillate crack that is actually at records, with a Gulf Coast system positioned into cheapening feedstock as crude falls. Same thesis, same catalyst and the same failure mode as MPC — record cracks mean-reverting when the ~7-8 mb/d of offline global capacity returns — which is why the pair together is 30 and not 45. I could not pull a fresh 8/28 quote before my research budget ran out, so I am sizing this at 10 rather than 15 and putting the same -18% stop on it, capping the leg at 1.8% of NAV.
JETSequityshort10.0%—−18%+25%Held at 10, and I want to correct the lazy bear case against it: crude falling 5% does NOT relieve airlines, because carriers buy the refined product, not the barrel, and the jet-fuel crack sits inside the same record complex I just increased my long exposure to. That is the point of the pair — MPC and VLO are long the crack, JETS short is short the crack's largest captive consumer, and both legs pay off on the same physical fact of refined-product scarcity. The industry has already conceded the math: the global sector nearly halved its 2026 profit forecast on Middle East fuel costs, US carriers' fuel bill ran $6.66bn in May at +85% y/y, roughly 20% of exported jet fuel is still stranded, and managements are cutting unprofitable routes and grounding less fuel-efficient aircraft. The demand leg strengthened independently this week: a Fed chair signaling hikes into a soft labor market pressures discretionary leisure travel, which flinches first when fares rise to cover fuel. What improved is that this no longer double-counts with a large crude long — cutting ERX removed the shared Hormuz failure mode I flagged last week, so this is a cleaner hedge than it was. Squeeze risk stays specific: the $2.5bn Frontier/Avelo federal liquidity ask with a possible government equity stake. Borrow costs ~30bps a year on 10%. Stop -18% caps it at 1.8% of NAV; take-profit held at +25%.
ERXequitylong8.0%—−20%+40%Cut 22 to 8 — the largest single change in the book and an admission that I was long the wrong end of the energy complex. I bought this on supply removal. Supply is coming back: Persian Gulf exports have recovered from a March low of 5-6 mb/d to 15-16 mb/d, the 8/24 sanctions package landed softer than its 'toughest in history' billing and oil fell on the news, and on 8/26 Iran and Oman announced a phased framework for a temporary 7-mile Hormuz corridor with joint mine-clearing. Brent went $93.86 to ~$88.5 and XLE $63.58 to $62.50. The market has reclassified this from a physical-supply threat to an economic confrontation, and a 2x fund with daily-reset decay is an expensive way to be stubborn about a thesis that has moved from base case to tail. Layer on a Fed that may hike: a firmer dollar and slower demand are both crude-negative. Why 8 and not zero — the re-escalation tail is genuinely live, not rhetorical. The June interim deal has lapsed, Iran publicly says the US is blocking the Hormuz agreement, the corridor is explicitly temporary and conditional on US compliance, mines are still in the water, and roughly 8 mb/d is still missing from the market. If that unravels, crude gaps up hard and 2x is the cheapest way to have owned the option. At 8% with a stop tightened -22% to -20% the leg costs at most 1.6% of NAV, a price I will pay rather than be flat a live geopolitical binary. Take-profit held at +40%.
SLVequitylong5.0%—−18%noneCut 10 to 5, the sharpest proportional trim in the book, because this is the leg whose written thesis was most explicitly a rate-cut bet — I raised it from 7 to 10 only last week citing 'a September cut at 91% implied odds.' Those odds are now roughly a coin flip on a HIKE. Silver is the higher-beta expression of the debasement trade, which means it is the higher-beta expression of a driver that just inverted, and its industrial half is precisely what a Fed deliberately slowing the economy damages — so both legs I bought it for weakened at once. It went flat on the week ($69.87 to $69.35) after an 8.8% run, so the gold/silver catch-up I paid up for has stalled rather than continued. I keep 5 rather than none because the structural supply deficit is independent of the Fed, silver is still well below its February mid-$80s high while gold sits near a record, and if the policy-error stagflation path is what Warsh is actually engineering then silver leads gold on the way up. But it is now a tail position, not a thesis position. Stop stays wide at -18%, capping it at 0.9% of NAV; this metal traded mid-$80s to $64 to $70 inside a year and anything tighter is noise.

Decision history — 7 recorded events
  1. 2026-07-27OPENEDOpening book registered · experiments/round3/allocations/opus5_unrestricted.json

    Outlook at registrationI expect this book to make money in the 8-20% range over the rest of 2026 if the oil supply regime holds, driven mostly by the ERX/MPC core, and to lose 8-12% if crude round-trips - the asymmetry comes from energy equities having repriced only about a third of the crude move, so they have far less to give back than crude does. Realised book vol on 2026 data is 11.4% annualised at a -0.18 SPY beta, so I should decouple from the index in both directions: I will likely lag a broad tech-led SPY rally and beat SPY in a rotation or a growth scare. At the Friday reassessments I am watching three things: (1) crude - if USO closes back below its June low I cut ERX to a token weight regardless of where the stop sits, because the whole book keys off the supply regime; (2) whether XLE's negative correlation to SPY persists, since it is doing a lot of the risk-management work and it is a regime feature, not a constant; (3) the semiconductor complex - if SMH stabilises and reclaims its June range I have to take the other side of my own call, cut the XLY short and add tech beta, because a resumption there would mean the July rotation was a shakeout rather than a leadership change. The risk I am most worried about is not the one the stops cover. It is that I have built a book whose energy core, XLY short, RTX leg and rate-sensitive XLF leg are all, underneath, the same single trade: a bet that the supply shock persists. My measured book correlations look diversified because they were measured inside the regime that the shock created. If crude resolves overnight on a geopolitical headline - the most likely single cause given the March and June round trips - roughly 60% of the book takes a correlated hit at the same gap, the -30% ERX stop fires at a price well below where it was set, and the healthcare and cash legs are the only things left standing. That is the scenario I would take a 12-15% NAV loss in, and no standing order prevents it; only cutting the weight before it happens does.

    Pre-registration backtest
    windows tested2026-01-02 to 2026-07-24; 2025-07-16 to 2025-12-31; 2025-01-02 to 2025-06-30
    strategy return pct2026H1 +31.95%; 2025H2 +4.33%; 2025H1 +5.25%
    benchmark return pct2026H1_SPY +8.74%; 2025H2_SPY +9.87%; 2025H1_SPY +6.31%
    max drawdown pct2026H1 -8.58%; 2025H2 -5.09%; 2025H1 -13.19%

    All figures are verbatim from tracker/round2.py --backtest on this exact construction. BE CLEAR ABOUT WHAT THIS IS AND IS NOT EVIDENCE FOR. The 2026-01-02 to 2026-07-24 window is almost entirely hindsight-contaminated and should be read as a construction check, not a result: ERX and MPC were selected precisely because energy led 2026, and XLV, XLF, RTX and AAPL were all picked off a trailing 3-month/1-month momentum screen run through the 2026-07-24 close, so every long leg knows the answer. The XLY short and the DOGE short were likewise selected on 2026 relative weakness. The +31.95% number therefore proves only that the engine prices the book the way I think it does and that the stops and take-profits behave as intended. The two 2025 windows are the honest out-of-sample tests, and there the book UNDERPERFORMS SPY on both: +4.33% vs +9.87% in 2025H2 and +5.25% vs +6.31% in 2025H1, the latter with a -13.19% drawdown against a +6.31% SPY. That is the expected shape - this is a bet on one specific 2026 macro regime (oil supply shock, rates up, long-duration tech de-rating), not a general-purpose alpha engine, and 2025H2 was the opposite regime (tech-led melt-up, flat energy), so a book that shorts consumer discretionary and levers energy has to lose there. I ran it anyway rather than tune it to pass, because passing 2025H2 would have required abandoning the thesis. Two mechanical findings worth recording: (1) leverage is unusually cheap in this sector - ERX realised 2.01x XLE on the year and 2.00x on the maximum drawdown, so the 2x wrapper cost roughly nothing, unlike SOXL (+190% YTD but -40% in a month at 123.6% vol) or FAS (0.78x XLF over 12 months); (2) the DOGE perp stop is NOT a reliable loss cap - in the 2025H2 run it gapped straight through both a -50% and a -60% stop level in a single close and returned only $9.74 of $40 margin, so the realistic worst case on that leg is close to the full 4% of NAV, which is why it is sized at 4%. Across the three windows the DOGE leg contributed +4.6pp, -3.1pp and +3.65pp versus an otherwise identical book without it. Engine-mechanics note: ERX is not in the engine's LEVERAGED_ETFS fee set so it is charged 2bps rather than 5bps on entry; the difference is about 0.7bps of NAV and the construction does not depend on it.

  2. 2026-07-31REBALANCEUnrestricted-retail resize (position caps lifted, free-internet research poll) · experiments/desk/unrestricted_resize_2026-07-30.json
    Stated reason (desk log)

    The thesis got materially stronger and my own book is what is holding it back. Since 27 July the account has made +0.36% while the mandate's core driver went vertical — crude +6.2% in a single session on the collapse of the ceasefire, with Hormuz still shut. The energy legs did their job (ERX +3.78% on the day) and the diversifiers ate the gains: AAPL -0.56%, XLV -0.61%, RTX -1.52%. So I am cutting the three legs that are no longer earning their weight and putting the capital into the two I actually believe in.

    CUT AAPL (7% to 0). It was bought as a hedge against the tech unwind reversing. It has stopped being that hedge: XLK fell 6.81% in July while AAPL made an all-time high and crossed $5trn. It has decoupled, so it will not protect me if semis keep unwinding, and it is not correlated to anything I need if energy works. On top of that it is a binary print tonight, at an all-time high, into a consensus price target 5% BELOW spot. That is a coin flip I am not paid to take.

    CUT RTX (7% to 0). This is the cleanest sell signal in the packet. RTX beat by 14% and RAISED full-year guidance on 23 July, and then fell — including -1.52% on the day crude gapped 6% on fresh Middle East strikes. A defence name that will not rally on a beat-and-raise INTO a widening war is fully priced. The 'coherent with the supply-shock regime' argument is true and irrelevant if the market refuses to pay for it.

    CUT XLF (11% to 0). It was the one leg with no thesis of its own — its stated job was to supply positive SPY beta so the book was not a pure short-market expression. I am scored on flat dollars, not tracking error, so paying 11 points for beta cosmetics is a waste. It is also the least coherent leg with the mandate: an oil shock at $89 Brent is stagflationary, and the NIM benefit from rising long yields is offset by the credit cost of a squeezed consumer.

    ADD ERX 22% to 32% (64% effective XLE). The single best piece of information I found is that XLE rose 1.88% on a 6.2% crude day. The equity market is pricing this as temporary and crude as mean-reverting; Hormuz has been shut since March and the ceasefire has already failed once. That skepticism is simultaneously my upside (equities have to converge) and my downside cushion (they cannot give back a move they never made — 2026 downside capture on crude down-days was 0.27x). ERX again realised exactly 2.0x with no decay, so I am getting the leverage cleanly. Stop stays at -30%, which caps this leg at 9.6% of NAV and corresponds to roughly a -15% XLE break.

    ADD MPC 9% to 16%. Highest-conviction single name and the only near-dated catalyst I own: 4 August, consensus EPS +184-199% y/y on record cracks, with management having pulled 40% of annual turnarounds into Q1 specifically to run at 94% utilisation into this window. The sell-side average PT of $301.59 is stale and sits below spot while the two most recent revisions are Goldman $376 and TD Cowen $357. Crack spreads are a genuinely different driver from crude beta (-0.16 correlation to SPY), so this is not just more ERX. I am sizing it BEFORE the print because the print is the reason. The -25% stop caps the leg at 4.0% of NAV, which is the price of admission for a stock up 71% YTD.

    ADD XLY SHORT 13% to 17%. The purest expression of the whole thesis and now doing double duty: $89 Brent is a consumer tax, and 39% of this ETF is AMZN plus TSLA — the two names carrying both the consumer squeeze and the AI-valuation de-rating that took XLK down 6.81% in July. At -0.38 correlation to XLE it is additive to the energy core rather than an offset, and it is my only real protection if the market breaks broadly. An ETF, so no single-name squeeze risk; 3% borrow; stop stays -18%.

    HOLD XLV at 20%. This is what lets me carry an 80% effective energy position. -0.07 correlation to XLE, 13.7% vol, +25% over one year, and State Street just moved healthcare to positive for Q3 on pipeline wins. Still unlevered on purpose — I do not want leverage on the ballast.

    HOLD DOGE short 3% at 3x. Unchanged logic and still free leverage: short perps pay zero funding while longs pay leverage x 10% APR. DOGE is at $0.0702, has not participated in any crypto bounce, and the loss is hard-capped at the 3% margin. Trimmed a point to fund the core.

    RISK FRAME. Effective energy exposure goes from ~53% to 80% of NAV. That is the mandate, executed at the size the new rules permit and the news now justifies. The single risk that kills this book is a durable ceasefire headline, because it hits ERX, MPC and the XLY short simultaneously. I have sized so that scenario is survivable rather than hedged away: with both stops firing the arithmetic bound is roughly -13 to -14% of NAV, against an upside of similar magnitude on a 15% XLE convergence — and I take that as skewed in my favour because energy equities never priced the spike they would have to give back. I am keeping 12% in cash at 4% as genuine dry powder rather than forcing it into the same trade; concentration where I have conviction, cash where I do not, and no third-best ideas in between. Filling on the next trading date — crude has already gapped and the equities have not followed, so I do not want to wait.

Filling on the next trading date — crude has already gapped and the equities have not followed, so I do not want to wait.

Both halves are now false: AMZN posted accelerating 37% AWS growth and rose 15.6% on 7/31, so 23% of my biggest short is an AI winner; TSLA is another 16% and expensive gasoline is a tailwind for EVs, meaning I was short a beneficiary inside an oil-tax trade. That leg has to go, and I am not paying to keep a short whose largest holdings are structurally on the wrong side of my own thesis. I am replacing it with the same trade expressed correctly. Airlines are the direct P&L counterparty to my refiner long: refiners earn the record crack, airlines pay it, jet fuel is +130% y/y at up to a quarter of opex, Spirit is already gone and the $2.5bn budget-carrier bailout has been publicly rejected by the administration — yet JETS trades near the top of its 52-week range. Second change: the evidence for refining margins hardened materially while the evidence for crude-beta convergence did not. That driver is refinery capacity shortage, not Hormuz, so it partly survives the ceasefire headline that is the single scenario that kills this book, whereas 2x crude beta does not. So I move six points out of ERX into VLO and keep the energy weight roughly where it was while shifting its centre of gravity from the leg I merely believe to the leg that is confirmed.     Weekly desk 2026-08-08: I am exiting refining entirely because the thesis was falsified by the people who run the companies. I sized MPC at 16% on the specific premise that management front-loaded ~40% of annual turnarounds into Q1 to run flat-out into this window, and I added VLO at 10% because its CEO had guided Q3 margins above Q2 with the binary print already behind it. On the 4 August call MPC told me Q3 carries ~$290mn of turnaround expense plus planned conversion-unit maintenance, that Q3 historically averages 95% capture against the 112% just printed, that early-Q3 margins are 'not at Q2 levels', that the jet-to-diesel spread has narrowed and that some Q2 drivers were 'not repeatable'. That is my sizing premise reversed by the issuer. The tape says the same thing louder: a 27% EPS beat ($17.73 vs $13.95, $5.1bn net income, margin doubled to $36.33/bbl) and the stock closed 8/7 at $301, below the ~$314 where I bought it. When a print that good cannot lift a stock, the forward money has already left. The commodity confirms it — the 3-2-1 crack's all-time $70-72 was a July peak, NY Harbor diesel has fallen from 84c on 10 July to ~60c and is now below its five-year average, distillate exports set an all-time weekly record, and EIA looks for significantly narrower cracks in 4Q26. Holding a token position with a dead thesis is worse than holding none, so both go. Second, Friday's payrolls print (-23k vs +80k, with ~100k of downward revisions to May and June, wage growth at a 2021 low) is a genuine regime break: an oil-driven inflation impulse landing on a contracting labor market. That is demand-negative for exactly the refined products I just sold, and it re-prices the Fed from a possible hike to cuts. The asset that wins in both tails of my own book is precious metals — it gets the haven bid if Hormuz escalates and the rate-cut bid if the strait reopens into a weakening economy — so gold becomes my largest single position at 20% with silver at 7% for beta to the same call. I take this in bullion, not miners: GDX/GDXJ have been squeezing shorts violently, which tells me the direction is right and the entry is extended, and I do not need levered operating gearing stacked on top of a 2x energy fund. Third, I keep the energy core because it is the one leg the week actually confirmed — crude fell ~5% and XLE gave up only ~1.5%, XLE rose 1.48% on Friday against a down tape, and energy is still the best-performing US sector. But 26% of a 2x fund is a 52% effective single-sector bet, and the de-escalation path is no longer a headline, it is a draft accord sitting in the Iranian parliament. Trimming to 20% keeps 40% effective XLE as my largest risk exposure while the labor data resolves. XLV goes up rather than down because the defensive rotation is now the trade and not merely the ballast — it closed 8/7 at $165.68 near a 52w high of $168.53, +29% on the year, 0.56 beta, and it is explicitly being bought as the haven for money leaving tech. JETS comes down to 6%: the demand half of the short improved on Friday but the cost half is going the wrong way, and I have the June precedent that a fuel-price drop puts 6-7% into airline stocks in one session. It is a labor-rollover short now, not a fuel-cost short, and it is smaller because it stays directionally additive to whatever energy exposure I still carry. Total turnover is roughly 65% one-way at ~2bps a side, about 1.3bps of NAV — cheap enough that being wrong for another week costs far more than the trade does.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-29: Two of my three stated premises broke this week and I am not going to hold positions whose written reasons are now false. The ERX thesis was supply removal — blockade plus 'toughest sanctions in history.' The sanctions landed softer than billed, Iran and Oman announced a phased Hormuz corridor framework with joint mine-clearing, Gulf exports have recovered from 5-6 mb/d in March to 15-16 mb/d, and Brent fell 5%+ to ~$88.5. That is my named worst tail arriving in slow motion rather than as a gap, which is the version where I actually get to act on it. The GLD and SLV sizes were justified in writing by '91% odds of a September cut'; Warsh used his first Jackson Hole speech to put rate HIKES in play, the two-year moved to 4.30%, and September hike odds are near 50%. Meanwhile the one leg that does not depend on either premise got materially stronger: the diesel crack printed a record $102.20, sits near $93-94, distillate inventories are at a 30-year low, 7-8 mb/d of refining capacity is offline, and MPC made an all-time high in the same week crude fell 5%. Cheaper crude is a feedstock tailwind to the crack, not a headwind. So I am selling the barrel and buying the bottleneck: ERX 22 to 8, MPC 12 to 20, new VLO 10, and the book's center of gravity moves from 'crude goes up' to 'refined products stay scarce' — a thesis that survives the de-escalation that is killing the old one and is paired against a short in the product's captive consumer. Metals go 30 to 19 because their engine reversed, not to zero, because gold held $4,608 through an explicitly hawkish Jackson Hole on record central-bank buying. Cash to 13 because a Fed that may hike makes 4%+ a real competing asset, and because I just cut my highest-conviction directional bet and do not want to force the proceeds somewhere to avoid looking idle.

WHAT IS DRIVING IT: FOMC on 29-Jul plus "chip worries spread." Investors rotating out of semis on hyperscaler capex discipline and signs China is closing the AI gap; Morgan Stanley calls a "hard remainder of 2026" for chips while JPMorgan calls it a buying opportunity; a Taiwan prosecutor detained an NVIDIA employee over server exports; Cathie Wood bought the dip; Burry/Cuban warning on Nvidia concentration.

THE DECISIVE OBSERVATION — DISPERSION, NOT INDEX VOL: MSFT and META both reported the night of 29-Jul and moved in OPPOSITE directions by 16 points. MSFT beat ($4.74 vs $4.24, Azure +43%, past $100bn ARR, and cut CY26 capex guide from $190bn to $175bn by extending datacentre life to 25 years) and is +8.83% after hours. META missed ($6.18 vs $7.22 consensus, Reality Labs -$4.6bn, capex raised to $130-145bn) and is -7.45% after hours. Weighting those in SPY (~4.5% and ~2.5%) they net to roughly +0.2% of index — single-stock variance is exploding while index variance is mechanically damped by offsetting constituents. That is the textbook falling-implied-correlation regime my mandate is built on, and it is now confirmed violently rather than merely inferred. AAPL and AMZN both report 30-Jul after the close, so the dispersion event has another leg tonight; NVDA is 26-Aug. Also picked up sell-side commentary that "low-volatility stocks are having a moment after a long stretch of underperformance," i.e. the factor rotation is early rather than exhausted.

HONEST NEGATIVE FINDING ON MY OWN BOOK: I re-ran the arithmetic on the TQQQ/SQQQ decay pair against my own recorded backtest (mean +0.29% of notional per 63 sessions = ~1.2%/yr) and it does NOT clear the 3% APR short borrow on both legs. Even grossing the decay up for the fact that QQQ realized vol is running at the 80th percentile (decay scales with sigma-squared, so maybe 2x the historical mean) it only gets to roughly break-even, against a backtested worst 63-day of -27.76% of notional. That is variance with no expected return, so the leg gets cut hard rather than upsized — which is the opposite of what "high vol in the tech complex" naively suggested.

StrategyClassified the current tape as a calm-index / high-dispersion regime (SPY 20d realized vol 11.65%, 34th percentile of two years, 10d/60d term ratio 0.80, versus QQQ 23.66% and XLK 30.67% at the ~80th percentile, and an implied-correlation proxy that has fallen from 0.54 to 0.34), and sized the book to that state: 60% in vol-targeted low-vol equity (USMV, SPLV) rather than the high-vol tech complex, 12% in SVXY to harvest the ~7-point gap between VIX 18.6 and SPY realized 11.65, a delta-neutral short-gamma pair of equal short TQQQ and short SQQQ to collect leveraged-ETF compounding decay, and 5% VIXY as convex crash insurance with a take-profit that monetises a spike.

Novelty statementI manage only a Round 3 book in this experiment, so the overlap constraint does not bind; the distinguishing construction here is a vol-regime book that hedges a policy-rate shock with measured positive-rate-beta legs (XLE, COMT) plus a floor-priced convexity leg, rather than with duration or gold, both of which my own regressions show carry the wrong sign against yields.

I am adding two points and not five because that test is right about the carry even when it is blind to the condition, and because the swap has to earn its place on the numbers, which it does: book volatility falls 5.00 to 4.75, max drawdown improves to -2.27%, the ten-worst-day average improves from -0.25% to -0.10%, and yield-up-day protection is unchanged at -0.08%. I am also adding to the leg that has lost the most since entry, -4.88%, and the justification is that it got cheaper while what it insures got more probable - the only good reason to add to a loser. Take-profit stays at +60% and I deliberately did NOT lower it despite the temptation to make it monetise an FOMC scare: I measured that VIXY captures 0.43 of a VIX percentage move on up days, so +60% implies roughly VIX 35 from a 14.51 base, whereas at VIX 18.6 the same trigger implied VIX 44. The falling VIX base already made this take-profit nine VIX points more reachable without my touching it, so tightening it further would be adjusting a parameter to feel active rather than because the design changed. No stop, for the reason that never changes: stopping out of insurance while it is losing money is the one thing insurance must never be allowed to do.

    Outlook at registrationI expect a low-volatility, positively-skewed-in-stress return profile: roughly 8-9% annualized portfolio vol against SPY's 11.65% realized, grinding out carry from the variance premium and the leveraged-ETF decay while the low-vol equity core supplies muted beta. In a continued calm melt-up this book should make money but lag SPY by several points a quarter; in a correlation spike it should be roughly flat to positive while SPY falls, because VIXY's convexity and the short-TQQQ leg both pay. Management at the weekly reassessment is explicitly regime-driven and mechanical: if SPY 20d realized vol rises through roughly 18% or the 10d/60d ratio moves above 1.3, I cut SVXY toward zero, cut the short-gamma pair (trend is its enemy), raise VIXY and cash, and rotate the equity core further toward USMV; if realized vol falls back under 10% with VIX still near 18 I add to SVXY and the decay pair. If dispersion compresses — the implied-correlation proxy climbing back toward 0.55 — the case for holding low-vol equity over the index weakens and I would move the core toward broader beta. The specific thing that would make me abandon the construction is realized vol printing above implied for several weeks, which would mean the premium I am being paid has gone negative.

    Pre-registration backtest
    windows tested2026-01-02 to 2026-07-24; 2025-07-16 to 2025-12-31; 2025-02-14 to 2025-05-30 (stress)
    strategy return pct2026H1 +4.14%; 2025H2 +1.69%; 2025_STRESS +5.47%
    benchmark return pct2026H1_SPY +8.74%; 2025H2_SPY +9.87%; 2025_STRESS_SPY -3.04%
    max drawdown pct2026H1 -4.75%; 2025H2 -2.85%; 2025_STRESS -8.07%

    Numbers are verbatim from `python3 tracker/round2.py --backtest <entry> <end> <file>` on this exact construction. The engine reports NAV $1041.42 / $1016.88 / $1054.73 on $1000. THE CENTRAL CAVEAT: a static allocation cannot switch regimes mid-window, which is the entire point of the strategy. These three windows therefore test whether the CURRENT regime call (calm index, high dispersion, wide variance premium) would have survived three different historical tapes — they do NOT test the switching rule, which only becomes visible across weekly reassessments in the live round. The book underperforms SPY by 4.6 and 8.2 points in the two rising windows and beats it by 8.5 points in the stress window; that asymmetry is the intended character, not a defect, but it means a sustained melt-up is the most likely way this book finishes behind. STOP DESIGN, FOUND BY ITERATION: an earlier candidate carried 30% stops on both leveraged-ETF legs and returned -5.92% with a -11.20% drawdown in 2026H1, because a whipsaw stopped out first one leg and then the other, twice converting a hedged pair into a naked directional short; removing the per-leg stops took the same window to +1.62% and the stress window from -0.05% to +7.83%. The pair is therefore risk-controlled by SIZE and by the natural floor on a short, not by stops. SVXY's stop was likewise widened from 18% to 25% after the tighter level fired at the March-2026 vol bump and locked in a loss the position then recovered. SHORT-VOL TAIL RISK, STATED PLAINLY: the accepted loss on a 1-day -21% / 5-day -34% SVXY event is about -3 to -4% of NAV after the stop, partly offset by VIXY, and the engine only checks stops at daily closes, so an intraday gap would fill worse than the stop level. In the stress window SVXY hit its stop and VIXY hit its take-profit (the engine prints these closures as LIQUIDATED) and the book still finished +5.47%, which is the hedge working as designed. Other caveats: no market impact or borrow-availability constraint on the leveraged-ETF shorts, flat 3% borrow and 10% funding, and daily-close granularity throughout.

  3. 2026-08-03REBALANCERegistered rebalance · experiments/round3/weeks/2026-08-03/opus5_volregime.json
    Registered book note — experiments/round3/weeks/2026-08-03/opus5_volregime.json

    Weekly desk 2026-08-01: I am not touching the equity core, which is a session old and needs no change; I am closing the two carry legs because one had its premise refuted overnight and the other was already refuted by my own arithmetic. SVXY existed to harvest the gap between implied and realized index vol. When I sized it that gap was ~7 points; after VIX collapsed 22% to ~16 against SPY realized of ~13-14% it is ~2-3 points. Getting paid 2-3 points to be short the tail is thin at the best of times, and this is not the best of times: the 10y just broke to 4.75% on $100 oil and an escalating Middle East conflict, which is precisely the macro shock that drags implied correlation back up and hurts a short-index-vol position most. The carry shrank and the tail fattened simultaneously, so the leg goes. The TQQQ/SQQQ pair is me correcting a documented mistake rather than reacting to news: on 7/30 I wrote that my own backtest gives it ~1.2%/yr on notional against 3% APR borrow on EACH leg — roughly -0.25% of NAV per year with a -27.76% worst 63-day — and then kept it at 7+7 anyway because it 'expressed the regime.' That was attachment to a narrative over my own numbers. It is a negative-carry structure whose best environment is chop and whose worst is trend, and an oil-and-rates shock is a trending catalyst, so the case only got weaker. Closing both costs about 26% turnover at ~2-2.5bps, roughly $0.07, and it is economically positive from day one: I stop paying 0.42%/yr of NAV in borrow and start earning 4% on the cash. VIXY goes up rather than down as the exact mirror of my 7/30 trim — I cut it then because buying insurance at VIX 20.66 right after a pop is paying up post-event, and the same insurance now costs ~22% less in VIX terms while the event it insures against became materially more likely. Buy convexity when it is cheap and the tail is fat; that is the discipline, and it is the reason I can still run an 78% low-vol equity core. The 16% cash is deliberate, not a residual: with my short-vol carry removed and a live geopolitical/inflation catalyst, dry powder that pays 4% is the right way to hold risk in reserve, and it funds adding to the core if the rate shock hands me a better entry. Net result is a simpler book, lower gross, no borrow, more cash yield, and my two best-evidenced legs plus a cheap hedge.

    Registered book note — experiments/round3/weeks/2026-08-10/opus5_volregime.json

    Weekly desk 2026-08-08: Two things moved enough to force this, and they point the same way. First, the volatility risk premium has closed: VIX 15.15 against SPY 20d realized 13.49% is ~1.7 points, versus a ~3-4 point norm, so index vol is no longer expensive - and Cboe implied correlation sits at a 23-year low (COR3M ~9-10, 52-week range 9.29-11.95), which is a bounded, mean-reverting quantity that can only normalise upward. Long index vol therefore pays if realized rises OR correlation normalises, and the compressed contango (VX6/VX1 1.062 vs a 1.15-1.20 norm) means I pay a third-to-half the carry I underwrote at entry. Cheaper insurance against a denser calendar - CPI 12-Aug, a stalled Hormuz fee dispute with Brent at $80, and a 15-16 Sep FOMC where a Warsh hike is still 44% priced after payrolls printed -23k with 103k of downward revisions. Second, and this is the correction I owe myself: I have been conflating vol targeting with owning low-vol stocks. Vol targeting scales exposure to the INDEX by the index's realized vol. USMV and SPLV buy their low vol by surrendering expected return and by parking 25% of SPLV in utilities ahead of a live hike; the index buys its low vol from diversification, which is free and is at a 23-year maximum precisely because correlation is at a 23-year low. At COR3M ~10 the S&P realizes 13.5% while its average constituent realizes far more - that makes SPY the cheapest carrier of equity risk in my universe right now, not USMV. My book was carrying only ~40 SPY-equivalent betas into a low-correlation, low-index-vol tape and made +0.97% while the index made +3.58% and tech made +7.2%. The fix is not to abandon defence, it is to take the permission the insurance already bought: raise index beta and raise the hedge together. Modelled across three states - calm melt-up, moderate scare, and a VIX-doubling shock - the new shape beats the old one in every one, because more cheap convexity is what makes more beta affordable rather than a substitute for it.

  5. 2026-08-17REBALANCERegistered rebalance · experiments/round3/weeks/2026-08-17/opus5_volregime.json
    Registered book note — experiments/round3/weeks/2026-08-17/opus5_volregime.json

    Weekly desk 2026-08-15: Two pieces of my own evidence turned against last week's construction and one turned against last week's arithmetic, so this is a correction rather than a view change - the regime call (calm index, violent components) is unchanged and this book expresses it better.

    First, the arithmetic. I built a 40% SPY core on 'index variance equals average constituent variance times correlation', arguing the cap-weighted wrapper is safer than its contents at a 23-year correlation low. That identity is an equal-weight identity. RSP realizes 9.79% at 20d and 10.92% at 60d against SPY's 13.33% and 13.93%, on the same tape in the same window - the equal-weighted index captures the diversification benefit I was describing while SPY's megacap concentration consumes most of it. I checked this was not a 20-day artefact before acting on it: over the trailing year RSP returned +21.8% against SPY's +22.0% with a smaller max drawdown (-7.9% vs -8.9%) and roughly 68% average downside capture across SPY's eight worst days. Identical return, a quarter less volatility, at all three horizons. If my mandate is return per unit of realized vol, RSP is simply the better vehicle for the exact thesis I already hold, so 30% moves to RSP and SPY keeps 20% because I am correcting an expression, not abandoning cap-weighted beta entirely.

    Second, the carry. VIXM/VIXY moved +3.9% in five sessions against a ~1.1%/week three-month average; netting each ETF's beta to spot leaves roughly a point a week of excess front-month decay, about 50% annualised. On 08-08 I explicitly justified upsizing VIXY to 11% on the claim that compressed contango had cut my roll cost to a third-to-a-half of the 43.8%/yr underwritten at entry. That claim is now false by my own measurement. Separately, the value case has thinned: VIX 14.25 against 10d realized 11.64% is 2.6 points of premium, near normal, and realized is falling faster than implied. I am not abandoning the hedge - VVIX at 87 is cheap convexity, SKEW rose to 138 in a week VIX fell, and the 15-16 Sep FOMC is a dated live binary inside my horizon - but a leg whose price of carry has doubled while its value case thinned should shrink to true insurance size, so 11% goes to 7% with the take-profit untouched.

    Third, SPLV. I kept it for tech-free diversification, but its protection is a rates bet and rates went the wrong way: ^TNX to 4.70 with ^IRX pinned at 3.70, a long-end-led steepening, which is precisely the inflation-expectations move an +7.9% Brent week produces. XLU -2.55% and SPLV -0.57% on the month confirm it. Once RSP is in the book, SPLV's broad-diversification role is redundant and only its concentrated utilities bet remains, so I exit it.

    What replaces it is the reason I am comfortable cutting the vol sleeve. XLE printed positive on five of SPY's eight worst days of the trailing year - better crash behaviour than SPLV's four of eight - while returning +49.2% over that year against SPLV's +6.2%. It is long the one macro shock actually running (Brent +7.9%, XLE +7.7%, USO +7.3% in a week the S&P gained 0.4% and VIX fell), and an energy-led inflation impulse is the single state where SPY, USMV and cash all lose together and only my hedges help. Sized at just 7% because it realizes 24.5% vol and because a leg that ran 7.7% in five sessions deserves respect, not enthusiasm. The net effect is a book with the same equity beta, materially less realized volatility, a hedge that earns rather than bleeds, and 18% cash at 4% into a live September Fed.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-22: The regime call was right and paid - the book made +0.30% while SPY lost 1.37% - so this is not a view change. It is a correction of where the hedge sits. I built this book to be hedged against an energy-inflation shock and then measured, for the first time, what each leg actually does when that shock arrives: regressed on daily 30y yield changes and ranked against the twelve largest yield-up days of the year, XLE is the ONLY long leg I own with positive rate beta (+1.86%/10bp at 60d, 8/12 positive, avg +0.72%), while SPY is -0.57, RSP -0.91 and USMV -0.40. The risk I named is now the one actually running - the 30y printed 5.31% this week, a 19-year high, on fiscal supply and term premium rather than policy - and I was carrying 7% against it and 68% exposed to it. Two dated catalysts sit inside the horizon and both push the same way: Bessent's Iran measures Monday 08-24 with Brent already +13% over two weeks on persistent Hormuz shut-ins, and Warsh's debut Jackson Hole keynote Friday 08-28, where September is now priced ~1-in-3 for a HIKE with three standing dissents already voted for one. So I double the macro hedge to 15% and fund it by trimming SPY from 20% to 14%, which is the same trade twice: a term-premium shock is a discount-rate shock and it hits the longest-duration cash flows hardest, which is precisely SPY's ~40% megacap concentration - XLK -3.53%, SMH -4.66%, Meta -7% in a week SPY lost 1.37% and RSP lost 0.49%. That is a mechanism, not the leadership forecast I said last week I did not have. I split the hedge across XLE and COMT rather than loading XLE alone because ~15% of XLE is refiners whose crack spreads can compress on exactly the transit-disruption shock I am hedging, and because XOM+CVX are 35% of the fund. Backtested over the trailing year the new book returns +14.02% against the current book's +11.83% at 5.03% vol vs 4.86% and -2.34% max drawdown vs -2.11%, with a better ten-worst-day average (-0.25% vs -0.37%) - more return, better crash behaviour, marginally more vol, and every variant I tested beat the incumbent, so the improvement is robust to the exact weights rather than fitted to them. VIXY stays at 7% despite finding the cheapest VIX convexity in two years (VVIX 2nd percentile, VIX minus rv20 at the 27th percentile against a 4.11 mean): I ran the sizing test before acting and across a year containing ten sessions worse than -1.5%, every extra point of VIXY above 7% cost more carry than it returned. Turnover is ~14% of NAV at 2bp a side, under a basis point all in.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-29: Two facts moved in opposite directions and the correct response is to move risk between hedges rather than to add or shed any. First, the driver behind my commodity hedge reversed: Brent peaked at 94.39 on 08-21 and closed 89.70, -4.97% off the high, and I raised XLE from 7% to 9% exactly seven days ago citing that rally by name. Sizing to a driver means cutting when the driver decays, so XLE goes to 6%. Second, the event my volatility hedge exists for became substantially more likely while its price fell to a sample floor: the desk reports Warsh's hawkish Jackson Hole repriced the 09-16 FOMC from 34% to 57% odds of a HIKE - twelve trading days inside my horizon, and a direction no equity leg I own is positioned for - while VVIX printed 82.90, the 0th percentile of my two-year sample. So VIXY goes from 7% to 9%. I am adding to the leg that lost the most since entry (-4.88%), and the reason is that it got cheaper while what it insures got more probable, which is the only good reason to add to a loser. I am deliberately honest that my headline argument for owning vol last week has weakened: VIX minus rv20 went from 1.98 points at the 27th percentile to 3.97 at the 41st, which is exactly average - the vol level is no longer cheap, only its convexity is, and that is why this is a two-point add rather than the five my enthusiasm wanted. My own backtest still says every marginal point of VIXY costs about a point of annual return. What makes the swap defensible rather than a hunch is that it improves the book on the measures I care about while leaving rate protection untouched: trailing-year volatility 5.00 -> 4.75, max drawdown -2.29 -> -2.27, ten-worst-day average -0.25 -> -0.10, twelve-yield-up-day average -0.07 -> -0.08. Everything else holds. I am not touching RSP after one week in which it lagged SPY by 58bp, because I wrote last week that I refuse to trade on a single window, and a week where megacap tech leads is precisely the state the equal-weight tilt is supposed to lag. Total turnover is 5% of gross, about a basis point of cost.

Financials (XLF at fresh ATHs on stress-test buybacks) and biotech (XBI, benefiting from a record $106B H1 M&A wave and a rotation into healthcare as a 'haven from tech') both showed relative strength on the down day, confirming that leg of the Round-3 book. Individual Round-2 names: SOFI and HOOD both beat Q2 estimates (SOFI record revenue +40% YoY/raised guidance; HOOD EPS $0.62 vs $0.43 consensus) but SOFI still sold off -8.9% while HOOD held up better (-3.2%, roughly in line with the tape); RKLB won a $266M Space Force contract but remains highly volatile ahead of 8/10 earnings; DUOL showed relative resilience (-0.6%) with three sell-side price-target hikes ahead of 8/5 earnings; CRSP is flat into an 8/3 print; ADBE (the short) squeezed +5.7% on a Q2 beat and a defensive AI acquisition (Topaz Labs), though Morgan Stanley's Underweight call on AI-disruption risk keeps the structural short thesis alive.
